d7116060ca08d060: AFTER sweeping both chambers of the US Congress, Democrats will turn their new investigative powers on the Trump family's business deals as they make what they call corruption a central part of a 2028 campaign for the White House.
Democrats seized control of both the Senate and House of Representatives in Tuesday's midterm elections, in which tens of millions of voters delivered a rebuke to President Donald Trump.
They wasted no time putting Republicans on notice.
"LAWYER UP," US Representative Robert Garcia, who is set to become chairman of the House Oversight Committee, posted on X late on Tuesday.
"Subpoenas," Senator Ron Wyden, who is expected to lead the Senate Finance Committee, wrote an hour later.
"Clear your schedule," US Representative Delia Ramirez said in a post addressed to several Trump administration officials.
Democratic committee leaders began outlining an oversight agenda on Wednesday that targets both the Trump administration and major corporations.
Wyden said he plans to scrutinise agreements between the Trump administration and pharmaceutical companies on drug pricing.
The Trump administration has denied any wrongdoing and on Wednesday it pushed back against the looming probes.

A White House official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said of the comments by Democrats: "They should be reminded that we still control the federal government and all of its powers," the official said.

Tech CEO and Republican mega-donor Elon Musk, Trump's sons and a swath of other Republican donors and contractors are likely to be swept up in investigations that could dominate the second half of Trump's term, according to Reuters interviews with around a dozen lawyers, members of Congress, congressional aides and political consultants.

"We expect a huge volume of aggressive and expansive investigations that will target both the administration and the private sector," said lawyer Rachel Cotton, a congressional oversight specialist at the Arnold & Porter law firm.

Analysts say that Democrats will have to walk a fine line between seeking to expose what they call unprecedented corruption under Trump and addressing voters' concerns about higher prices for consumer goods and gasoline.
Whether Democrats succeed will have major implications for a so far wide-open race to succeed Trump in the 2028 presidential election.

"The Democrats will be less concerned with Trump and more about tying the corruption to the whole administration and ultimately to the entire" Republican party, said Sarah Longwell, a former Republican strategist and longtime Trump critic, adding that part of the aim will be to erase a political path for Trump administration officials.
Longwell said that Democrats could also benefit politically from probing how Republicans handled information around the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
"Even if it's more political theater than anything else, any time we're talking about Epstein, Trump's popularity is suffering," she said.
Yet Democrats risk overplaying their hand, said Republican consultant Ron Bonjean.
"Voters are more concerned about affordability," Bonjean said.
"If the vengeance that Democrats are seeking overwhelms their legislative agenda then they're likely to have a very short legislative majority"
Some 48 per cent of registered voters in a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted nationwide from Thursday last week through Monday said cost of living was the top issue determining their vote.
But voters have also expressed concern about Trump's personal enrichment amid his family's flurry of crypto and real estate deals.
In an August Reuters/Ipsos poll, some 69 per cent of Americans said they thought his private business interests were influencing his presidential decisions.

For any investigations to succeed, Democrats will have to avoid getting bogged down in litigation with a combative White House and keep what could be a raucous coalition in line, lawyers and congressional aides said.

"There will be a lot of pressure on Democrats to issue subpoenas early. But the juice has to be worth the squeeze for whatever they decide to litigate," said lawyer Kimberly Hamm with Morrison Foerster.
The House, which will likely move faster than the Senate, should be narrow in its asks and strategically try to limit the potential objections from the White House, said Hamm.

Corporations are prime targets for investigations because, unlike the White House, they cannot claim their activities are protected by executive privilege, although the White House could step in and claim they are, lawyers said.
Winning the Senate gives Democrats a "broader field" on which to play, said lawyer Mike Fragoso with Torridon Law.
"The question is how willing and able they will be to pick their targets and focus on them."
* The writer is from Reuters

df1af979e44b9e93: PARIS: Carlos Alcaraz gained a measure of revenge on Ben Shelton on Sunday as the seven-time Grand Slam champion beat the American 7-6 (7/5), 7-5 to win the Paris Masters for the first time.
In defeating the man that ended his US Open title defence earlier this season, the 23-year-old Spaniard claimed the ninth 1000-level title of his career.
Unlike their five-set quarter-final epic in New York two months ago, the clash in Paris lasted just under two hours.
Ahead of the ATP Finals, which run November 15-22 in Turin, world number three Alcaraz now holds five tour-level titles this year – only the injured Jannik Sinner has more with six.
In Italy, he will be seeking a first coronation at the season-ender.
After winning two French Opens and now the Paris Masters, Alcaraz is undefeated in title matches in the city.

But not for the first time in the French capital, Alcaraz won the title by saving match points en route – this time against Taylor Fritz in the quarter-finals in scenes reminiscent of his iconic Roland Garros final win against Italian Sinner last year.

For world number four Shelton, it was a first defeat in a Masters final after winning his two previous appearances in showpiece matches at that level– both coming in the last two editions of the Canadian Open.
'Ten out of ten'
Serving at 1-2 in the first set, Alcaraz flirted with danger as he offered up four break points, but dug in to secure the hold when Shelton misfired at the end of a seven-minute long game.

Shelton then found himself two break points down in the seventh game but responded with a perfect drop volley and blistering passing shot to bring up deuce, before holding and keeping his nose in front.
Although both players threatened on the other's serve and drew repeated gasps from the crowd with some audacious shot-making, the opener nonetheless required a tie-break to separate them.
A Shelton error at 4-4 followed by a leaping backhand smash by Alcaraz brought up two set points.

The first came and went when Alcaraz thundered the ball into the top of the net cord and the expectant arena froze in time as it rose and fell in seeming slow motion, only to land on the Spaniard's side of the court.
Alcaraz was not to be denied a second time, however, as Shelton overcooked a forehand on the next point to cede the opener.

At 2-2 in the second set, Shelton let out a bellow of frustration after missing a groundstroke at 15-30 on Alcaraz's serve, but the American could smile at the end of the game as a double fault and missed forehand produced the first break of the match.

Alcaraz had said after booking his spot in the final that his reflexes would need to be "ten out of ten" when facing Shelton's serve and they were just that three games later as he levelled the set at four-all.

A deft exchange of angled drop shots ended by an Alcaraz winner down the line brought the Spaniard's finger to his ear and the crowd again to their feet as Shelton suddenly found himself serving to keep the final alive.
He did so at the first time of asking but when required to serve again to force a breaker, Shelton cracked as Alcaraz again pounced to seal the title with a flicked backhand winner. — AFP

5f4e9a13912ccb79: WASHINGTON: Tech megabillionaire Elon Musk and President Donald Trump's newly appointed White House chief of staff, Stephen Miller, will likely be targets of congressional probes when Democrats take control of Congress in January, a senior lawmaker said on Sunday.

California Representative Robert Garcia, who is in line to chair the powerful House Oversight Committee next year after Democrats' sweeping midterm election victory, said investigations will focus on Musk's involvement in the Department of Government Efficiency's firing of federal workers last year, and Miller's role in Trump's hardline immigration crackdown.
"I think there's a lot of interest, not just from our committee, but from committees across the Congress to speak to Mr. Musk," Garcia told CNN's "State of the Union."
Miller — whom Garcia called the architect of a "horrific, unjust" immigration policy — has been promoted to White House chief of staff, Trump said on Friday.
"Stephen Miller is at the center of the major policy decisions that are happening in the administration, and so it does deserve oversight and investigation," Garcia said.

The crackdown on immigration, which included operations in which two people were fatally shot in Minnesota by federal agents, has proven widely unpopular. A Reuters/Ipsos poll in October found that only 37 per cent approved of Trump's handling of immigration, down from 50 per cent when he took office.

Voters delivered a historic rebuke to Republicans in Tuesday's midterm election, but with Miller as White House chief of staff, the Trump administration is expected to ‌continue its aggressive approach to immigration enforcement, amplify cultural conflicts and give no ground to a Democratic-controlled Congress, say officials and experts who spoke to Reuters.

Hakeem Jeffries, who will become speaker of the US House in January, said on Sunday that Democrats would support a measure to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, a congressional process that could remove him from office.
Representative Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican, has said he will reintroduce articles of impeachment against ​Hegseth soon. Jeffries said he is a "hard yes" on backing that measure.

"Pete Hegseth has got to go... I believe there will be incredibly strong support for that resolution," Jeffries told ABC's "This Week," citing the defense secretary's oversight of the unpopular Iran war launched by Trump in February, which has led to a spike in gas prices.

Attorney General Todd Blanche signaled on Sunday that the Trump administration was prepared to battle the Democrats in Congress, calling threats by some Democrats to target administration officials and allies "not something we can tolerate in this country."
"If that's what this new incoming leadership wants to do, we are ready," Blanche said. "If you work in this administration, you have a lawyer. It's me." — REUTERS
5d71332363864274: LONDON: Chelsea suffered a shock 1-0 defeat at Premier League strugglers Sunderland, while Liverpool got back on track with a 3-1 win against lowly Crystal Palace on Sunday.

An own goal from Leif Davis in the 46th minute increased Bournemouth's lead and Jack Clarke's 73rd minute penalty wasn't enough to rescue Ipswich.
In Sunday's late game, Manchester United manager Michael Carrick cannot afford a defeat against Aston Villa at Old Trafford as he fights to save his job ahead of the international break.
United are without a victory in their last seven league games and have won just once in the top-flight this term.
They ended a miserable nine-match winless run in all competitions by coming from two goals down to beat Roma 3-2 in the Champions League on Tuesday. — AFP

34a69adb6dd2c290: PETALING JAYA: Filmmaker Isa Batharul Zaman, popularly known as Isa Isarb, says he was recently detained by Indonesian authorities and accused of being a Malaysian spy when he was arrested while filming forest fire protestors.

He said he was in Indonesia to film a documentary about the haze and had stopped on his way to an area affected by forest fires. Some 10 to 15 officers approached him and asked if he was “Isa Batharul”, making him uneasy as he was not generally known by his birth name.
“We were then arrested for allegedly misusing our tourist visas. We were told that our visas did not allow us to film or be present at demonstrations,” he was quoted as saying by Sinar Harian today.
Isa said he was questioned at a police station, where he was asked to state the real reason he had come to Indonesia, and spent the night in a lockup.
He said he was accused of being a spy the next day, with the authorities citing his conversations with several Malaysian politicians as evidence.

“The conversations they referred to were between me and the Malaysian deputy prime minister’s team, as well as Muar MP Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman and communications minister Fahmi Fadzil. Those conversations were related to interviews I had sought for the documentary I was filming,” he said.
Isa said his invitation to Parliament earlier that week had also heightened suspicions during his questioning.
“I was invited there solely to interview the MP. The location was chosen to accommodate his busy schedule, especially since he had recently got married,” he said, referring to Syed Saddiq.
He said he was allowed to return to Malaysia because of Putrajaya’s good relations with Jakarta.
Isa said he plans to release his documentary on his YouTube channel on Nov 16, after the Melaka polls, but added that he does not want the matter to be politicised.

But people are hungry for edgy. This is how music lost its power. It became about the brand, grosses and… The most revered acts of all time were not necessarily the ones who hoovered up the most money.
So you’ve got to say no to those checks being offered. For your own benefit. You can’t be above the public, but right down in the pit with people.
This is what the Millers are trying to escape.

But that ship sailed over a decade ago. In today’s world everybody has a voice and everybody is equal. You’re grist for the mill. If you’re too big for your britches, if you’re a lyin’, stinkin’, scumbag, the minions are going to go wild on you online.
Everything we were told was true has been flipped. That the oligarchs dictated and…
Funny how all those companies left California for Texas, what now? Did you see the mayor of Houston just decoupled from ICE? If the police stop undocumented people, they’re not going to alert ICE.
Give the guy credit for adjusting. Unlike Agent Orange.
This is why you play the game, because you never know how it will turn out. No one expected a victory this big, no one expected the country to be this pissed.
So now…
We all want to return to business as usual, stop focusing on Washington, D.C., but before that happens…
We’ve got work to do.
Or as the Stones would say…WE’VE GOT THE TURD ON THE RUN

260afbe58650886a: CAIRO: Two trains collided south of the Egyptian capital on Sunday, derailing several carriages, killing four people and injuring dozens, according to the authorities.
Egypt's railway authority said a train travelling from Giza to Fayoum crashed into the rear of another service heading south from Cairo to the city of Aswan.
The Health Ministry said an initial count put the toll from the crash at four passengers killed, with 88 others being treated for injuries in hospitals around the Giza area.
State-owned media had earlier reported 120 people were wounded, without clarifying the severity of their injuries.

President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said he was following the accident "with great concern" and had directed authorities to conduct an urgent investigation to "hold accountable anyone found to have been negligent".
Emergency crews used cranes to remove the wreckage, the authority said.
Authorities said they had launched an investigation into the cause of the crash, which occurred in Giza's Al-Ayyat area, the site of Egypt's worst-ever rail disaster.
In 2002, more than 370 people were killed when a fire swept through a train carrying holidaymakers south of Cairo.
In 2009, multiple train crashes in the area killed dozens.
Egypt's 110 million people depend heavily on rail transport, but the network — one of the largest in Africa — has suffered repeated deadly accidents.

Over the past decade, Egypt has poured billions of dollars into updating its transport infrastructure, including new highways and high-speed rail lines, but has yet to overhaul much of its ageing rail network.
28c357dcdb50fbc1: GENEVA: EU Commissioner for Equality, Preparedness and Crisis Management Hadja Lahbib on Sunday called for greater access for humanitarian aid to the Gaza Strip as heavy rains flooded displacement camps, worsening conditions for families already facing a severe humanitarian crisis, Anadolu Ajansi reported.

"The rain makes a crisis that was already unbearable worse," she said.
Lahbib noted that humanitarian organisations were continuing their operations despite the storm but stressed the urgent need for additional assistance.

c76352dd7464414b: JAKARTA: A crew member of a helicopter battling Indonesian wildfires was killed on Sunday when the aircraft crashed into a river while scooping up water for an airborne drop, a local disaster agency said.

The crash in Borneo's South Kalimantan province was the second in days involving a firefighting aircraft, after a military helicopter plunged into the waters off Borneo on Wednesday, killing three people.

Two Australian pilots survived Sunday's crash and were "safe", Berton Panjaitan, a spokesman for the National Disaster Mitigation Agency, told AFP earlier on Sunday. Further details of their condition were not immediately available.
Dramatic video footage showed the firefighting helicopter being slowly dragged downwards after filling its bucket in the Barito River, eventually plunging nose-first into the water.

"A joint search and rescue team recovered the final victim at 6:08 pm local time during a diving operation involving four divers," a statement released by the search and rescue office in the provincial capital, Banjarmasin, on Sunday evening said.

The Southeast Asian archipelago has been struggling for months to control blazes that have burned through large swathes of Sumatra, Borneo and Papua, causing choking haze that drifted to neighbouring Malaysia, East Timor and Singapore.
"This incident occurred while the air fleet was conducting a water-bombing operation," spokesman Berton told AFP.
The Eurocopter EC225LP Super Puma belonged to a company the disaster mitigation agency had contracted for water-bombing operations, he said.
On Wednesday, a helicopter carrying eight people crashed during a mission to fight fires in Tanjung Puting National Park, home to animals including critically endangered Bornean orangutans.
That crash also occurred while the aircraft was scooping seawater for water bombing, according to an army statement that said the cause was under investigation.

Aside from ground-based firefighters, Indonesia has relied heavily on air operations to fight the fires, which have destroyed more than 1.9 million hectares, according to deforestation monitor Nusantara Atlas.
The fires are driven in part by a strong El Nino weather phenomenon, which typically causes drought in Indonesia.

430522e4cea2971d: KOTA BHARU: Sembilan jajahan di Kelantan diramal berkemungkinan dilanda banjir bermula hari ini hingga 11 Nov, susulan amaran hujan berterusan yang dikeluarkan Jabatan Meteorologi Malaysia (MetMalaysia).

Pusat Ramalan dan Amaran Banjir Negara (PRABN), Jabatan Pengairan dan Saliran (JPS) memaklumkan jajahan terlibat ialah Kota Bharu, Tumpat, Bachok, Machang, Pasir Mas, Pasir Puteh, Tanah Merah, Kuala Krai dan Jeli.

"Bagi jajahan Kota Bharu, kawasan berisiko melibatkan Lembangan Sungai Kelantan, manakala di Tumpat membabitkan Lembangan Sungai Golok termasuk Sungai Golok, Sungai Pengkalan Nangka, Sungai Mentua dan Sungai Kelaboran," menurut kenyataan.

45b754c01759e6ff: PETALING JAYA: Seorang Ahli Parlimen Sabah menggesa siasatan dijalankan berhubung projek bekalan elektrik luar bandar di kawasannya, yang dipercayai terbengkalai sejak 2019, sekali gus menyebabkan ribuan penduduk tidak mendapat bekalan elektrik yang sempurna.

FMT sedang berusaha mendapatkan maklum balas daripada KKDW berhubung perkara ini.

9e1bf8382febeec5: SITTING astride the Strait of Malacca in the centre of Southeast Asia has brought the country immense blessings, from being a shipping hub since time immemorial to being an essential aviation centre for regional and international airlines in more recent times.

With this has come trade and tourism, making Malaysia a strategic magnet for people from all over. With blessings, though, usually comes a potential curse; that we attract also less savoury characters and those who have a criminal bent.

We need, therefore, not just to reap the clear economic advantages of our strategic location but also to take care that it does not become a strategic weakness. The same connectivity that makes the country a regional trade, aviation and logistics hub also provides opportunities for drug traffickers to move their illicit cargo across borders.

This being the case, Home Minister Datuk Seri Saifuddin Nasution Ismail let on that the cabinet has approved a joint memorandum between the home and transport ministries on Aug 19 for the implementation of a comprehensive, short to medium and long-term action plan on Security Improvement and Mitigation to strengthen phased-in security controls and screening at Kuala Lumpur International Airport (KLIA) and other international entry points.
Malaysia's proximity to the Golden Triangle, one of the world's major drug-producing regions, puts it in a particularly vulnerable position. This is not merely a theoretical concern.

In March, police seized more than 3.4 tonnes of methamphetamine worth an estimated RM170 million in the Klang Valley. The drugs had reportedly entered through northern Peninsular Malaysia before being stored in rented houses.
In November, police also linked a Hong Kong drug seizure to a syndicate that had used Malaysia as a transit point before the drugs were despatched through KLIA and Penang International Airport.

The challenge is that enforcement cannot be confined to airports. Ports, coastal waters, land crossings, warehouses and logistics facilities all need to be part of a well-coordinated security strategy.

The government's 17-point security improvement and mitigation plan for KLIA and other international entry points is a timely step in the right direction. However, the government will need to ensure that implementation is measurable, adequately funded and continuously evaluated.

We basically need to ensure a fool-proof protective shield covering virtually the entire country, given that an increased security focus on airports will incentivise the drug syndicates to probe for other vulnerable spots along our lengthy coastline as well as land borders.

We simply cannot afford to become a convenient stopover for the international narcotics trade. Our connectivity must be protected at all costs, not exploited. Intelligence gathering and sharing, border screenings and enforcement coordination must all be beefed up without compromising legitimate trade and travel in and out of the country.

There must be no let-up. As the minister rightly said, the police, through the Narcotics Crime Investigation Department, are intensifying efforts against the illicit trade through the entire syndicate network.

55efd18d2ef193c9: LAST week's US$6.3 billion Binance heist is prompting insurers to scrutinise cryptocurrency companies' security more closely, with underwriters expected to probe if clients are vulnerable to a similar attack when they seek new coverage or renew existing policies, industry insiders and experts said.
Insurers are not expected to broadly retreat from the crypto sector or reduce the availability of coverage.

But the largest crypto theft on record could bring tougher scrutiny of crypto firms' exposure to Binance and any weaknesses identified in the attack, which the Federal Bureau of Investigation has blamed on a North Korea-linked group.
The attack underscores the limits of the insurance coverage available for the fast-growing over US$2.5 trillion industry.
No available crypto insurance could cover a loss of the scale suffered by Binance, experts said, while many policies have exclusions for state-backed cyberattacks.
Grand View Research projects the global crypto insurance market will grow to US$192.7 billion by 2033 from US$13.8 billion this year.

"Insurers will be asking questions specific to Binance. Their first question will be very simple: what is your exposure to them and do you have any money with them?" said David Rogers, managing director of financial institutions at Gallagher.

According to a report that Binance published this week, hackers used a bogus job interview and software hidden in an ​advertisement to compromise the computers of two Binance software engineers before using a third computer to drain US$6.3 billion worth of crypto.
The world's largest crypto exchange detailed a multi-stage hacking endeavour that began in June and set off a series of security breaches culminating in the theft on Thursday.
Following the attack, crypto exchanges quickly moved to bolster their defences and push for greater information-sharing across the industry.
The implications of their insurance will likely become clear at their next renewal, executives said.
Policies typically run for a year, giving underwriters an opportunity to reassess a client's risks, seek updated information and impose new security requirements before agreeing to extend coverage.

Jacqueline Quintal, Marsh's financial institutions and digital asset industry leader, did not anticipate material changes in insurance capacity, pricing or coverage, but for insurers to ask clients more questions, including whether they could be exposed to a similar attack.
She said one would not want to be the person who, a week after this happened, renews or writes a crypto risk and then the same thing happens.
The scrutiny could extend beyond a general assessment of whether cybersecurity controls to specific weaknesses uncovered by the Binance investigation.
Insurers may seek assurances that similar vulnerabilities do not exist elsewhere during renewal.

"If it becomes apparent from the investigation into this hack that there was a very specific weakness or flaw in Binance's security, then other insureds can certainly expect to see a requirement for that weakness or flaw to be resolved," said Peter Hardy, a London-based insurance lawyer at Reed Smith.
The scale of the Binance heist also highlights the limits of the protection available to cryptocurrency businesses.

"A loss of this magnitude prompts underwriters to re-examine their whole crypto book, not just the affected insured, reassessing aggregate exposure, wordings and sub-limits across the portfolio," Alan Lyons, co-chair of the Insurance, Reinsurance & Dispute Resolution Group at Herrick, said.
The predictable response is tighter wordings and clearer exclusions, he said.

North Korea has for years used state-linked cyber units for espionage and financial theft, according to US and South Korean authorities and cybersecurity experts. Pyongyang has denied the allegations.
North Korea's involvement could complicate insurance claims, as cyber policies placed at Lloyd's have generally required exclusions for state-backed attacks since 2023.
The Binance loss also exceeds the capacity of any available policy, he said.
"If an attack is attributed to a state, insurers may dispute or deny claims. The effectiveness of these exclusions in a major, geopolitically driven loss remains untested."
That's a challenge, given the industry is expected to continue expanding with the growth of custody services and wider adoption of cryptocurrencies.
Even multiple policies responding would be insufficient to cover a loss of this scale.
"Potential new entrants to the market may be more cautious but the market will steady itself and in time bounce back," Hardy said.

4ff257b87e77617a: KUALA TERENGGANU: Terengganu's Bersekutu Bersatu wing has no objection to the state government's proposal to appoint a Gerakan member as an appointed assemblyman.

744c01fbb15b8c08: ACCUSATIONS of police illegally wiretapping Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto and the possible impeachment of his vice-president have exposed fresh tensions in the relationship between Prabowo and his influential predecessor.
Prabowo, a former general with a checkered past, shares a long and complex history with Joko Widodo, the former president better known as Jokowi.
Jokowi defeated Prabowo twice in the 2014 and 2019 presidential elections.
He then appointed Prabowo as defence minister. That helped rebuild Prabowo's reputation after accusations of rights abuses and ended a de facto ban on him travelling to the United States.
Prabowo, who denies any wrongdoing, then won tacit support for his 2024 presidential bid from Jokowi, who was barred by term limits from running again.
Key to that support was his promise to continue Jokowi's legacy projects including building a new capital city, Nusantara.

During that election, Jokowi faced allegations of breaching ethics and meddling ahead of the polls, including in a court's last-minute decision to change election rules, which allowed his son to become Prabowo's running mate.
Jokowi's brother-in-law was head of that court at the time and was reprimanded by an ethics panel for intentionally allowing "intervention from an external party".
Jokowi has rejected those allegations.

In addition to picking Jokowi's son, Gibran Rakabuming Raka, as his running mate, Prabowo installed a number of Jokowi loyalists in his administration in what analysts said was a bid to tap into some of Jokowi's huge support base.
But cracks in their relationship began to appear when he removed or reassigned Jokowi loyalists and technocrats in a series of reshuffles that began in September 2025.

Among those removed was Sri Mulyani Indrawati, who served as Jokowi's finance chief for eight years. More recently, Listyo Sigit Prabowo (no relations to the president), a former police chief who became the president's chief of staff in October, was sacked this week after he was arrested in the wiretapping scandal.
Investigators have not said what they believe is the motive for the wiretapping.
Prabowo has also only approved 48.8 trillion rupiah in funding for the Nusantara project until 2029, about 60 per cent of what Jokowi spent between 2022 and 2024.

In September, a group, including an election monitoring organisation, petitioned the Constitutional Court to review Gibran's eligibility in the 2024 election, arguing that he did not have the appropriate credentials.
There is no apparent connection between the group and Prabowo.
The court last month ruled that Gibran's education diplomas issued overseas did not meet election requirements, but the judges also said he could not be removed from office.

In a separate complaint, the Supreme Court ruled last month that a key education document Gibran used during the election was invalid, according to local media reports. The court has not published its full ruling.
Lawmakers are looking at launching a parliamentary inquiry into the matter, which analysts believe to be the first step towards an impeachment.

According to two people with knowledge of Jokowi's thinking, Jokowi was disappointed that neither Prabowo nor members of his coalition showed any support when questions were raised about Gibran's educational credentials.
Jokowi's assistant did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.

Gibran also publicly apologised twice that Prabowo's signature free meals for schools programme had resulted in cases of food poisoning — a position that ran counter to the president's, the people said.

2872f5913f4931c9: JERUSALEM: Israel's former military chief Gadi Eisenkot was set on Sunday to be given the tough task of forming a government, with weeks to cobble together a coalition to replace Benjamin Netanyahu, the country's longest-serving prime minister.

Eisenkot, 66, a political novice who has vowed to bridge Israel's deep polarisation under Netanyahu, was due to meet President Isaac Herzog, who will formally give him the mandate to form a government, with an initial deadline of 28 days.

Eisenkot, born to a family of working-class Moroccan immigrants, would be the first Sephardic prime minister — a descendant of Jews from the Middle East or North Africa — in a country long dominated by an Ashkenazi elite with ties to Europe.

Netanyahu, who has been prime minister on and off for nearly two decades and has led wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran since the Oct 7, 2023 attacks, lost support in last month's election, but no side claimed an outright majority.
In consultations with Herzog last week, Eisenkot received recommendations from parties accounting for 67 lawmakers, against 46 for Netanyahu.

But the vote count included Israeli Arabs, whose seat haul surged to a historic high amid anger over Netanyahu's government, which includes far-right firebrands who have openly sought to marginalise the community.
Wooing the ultra-Orthodox

Avigdor Liberman, a former Netanyahu aide turned sharp critic who nonetheless shares his hawkish views, has been adamant against any alliance with Israeli Arabs, descendants of Palestinians who stayed after Israel's creation in 1948.

Taking back one of his signature campaign pledges, Liberman instead voiced openness to an alliance with ultra-Orthodox Jews, whose almost singular priority is ensuring that they remain exempt from military service.

The exemption for the ultra-Orthodox — whose two main parties had been aligned with Netanyahu but could help Eisenkot secure a majority — has been a source of growing resentment among many Israelis as reservists serve multiple tours of duty.

Liberman said on Sunday he still backed conscription for all Israelis but had to make "difficult decisions" in pursuit of the higher priority of ousting Netanyahu, who faces corruption charges that could land him in jail if he loses power.
But he remained adamant that he would never ally with Israeli Arabs.
"I will not lend a hand to the establishment of such a government, which in my view will harm security and bring Netanyahu back to power," Liberman wrote on X.
Liberman, whose party has seven seats and is the smallest within the opposition bloc, denied speculation that he was trying to engineer a deadlock that could result in him becoming prime minister.
Born in Moldova and with a party base originally made up of Russian-speaking immigrants, Liberman said commentators' views on his motives had "sometimes a distinctly racist tone".

Naftali Bennett, the second strongest opposition leader after Liberman, has also been outspoken against the ultra-Orthodox community's military exemption and has remained silent since Liberman's about-face.
'National emergency'
Eisenkot has called for a "national emergency" government that would remove Netanyahu, calling him "a fundamental threat to the very existence of Israeli democracy".
He has ruled out a unity government with Netanyahu, who has repeatedly called for a broad coalition with himself at the helm.

Eisenkot appears to be suggesting that he is willing to start with a minority government — relying on outside votes from Israeli-Arab parties — while continuing to seek a stable government with majority support.

Assaf Shapira, a political expert at the Israel Democracy Institute, said Eisenkot would face an especially fragile government if it had only 48 lawmakers, even if others promised to keep it in power.
"To pass laws, you need strong support from other parties," Shapira said, explaining that an Eisenkot minority government would be forced into extensive negotiations on every piece of legislation.
Eisenkot has vowed to repair Israel's international reputation and put an end to rampant violence against Palestinians by extremist West Bank settlers supported by Netanyahu's government.
He has warned Netanyahu that he does not have the mandate for another attack on Iran but has also largely backed his war decisions.

Having commanded the military during the 2006 war with Hizbollah, Eisenkot devised the so-called "Dahiya doctrine", which calls for massive force against civilian infrastructure where enemies operate — a policy critics say amounts to a war crime.
In Tel Aviv, Neri Bar-On, who works in educational technology, said he expected Eisenkot to succeed in forming a government.
"But the problems run deeper," he said.
"The country is facing a massive internal conflict; even if he manages to form a government, it won't solve the underlying issues."

a9358c545b330361: LETTER: This is my third year not being able to celebrate Deepavali at home, in a part of the United Kingdom where the festival is not even routinely known or recognised.
I found myself on the couch at half past 10 in the evening, Greenwich Mean Time, tucked under a blanket because it is miserably cold, scrolling through YouTube.
And what do i find but a repost by Petronas. Their Deepavali advertisement from 2003.
It was quite a sensation back then, and remains one of their most memorable.
The one where Patti innocently asks Sam, in Tamil, what sort of a name Sam is, only for him to reveal that his actual name is Muthusamy Karrupiah.
I was eleven back then. A primary school pupil. My father was still alive and well. I had no ambitions, no financial obligations or worries. I was simply a child.
Now, over two decades later, I am a grown adult, navigating the uncertainties of life as an international medical graduate trying to build a life in the UK.
Rewatching it brought back memories of a better time.
Of those halcyon days, as one would say, when life seemed so much simpler and the people i loved were still around.
And the message at the end? "The world is changing, but we will always be proud of who we are."
As an 11-year-old, i probably never gave those words a second thought. As an adult, I finally understand what they mean.

I am proud to call myself a Malaysian Tamil, and that will remain my identity no matter where life takes me. Living abroad also made me realise how much of myself remains rooted in the country i call home.
Perhaps that is the strange thing about growing older. Things that once seemed insignificant acquire an entirely different meaning when revisited through the eyes of an adult.
An advertisement that once interrupted my grandmother's favourite Tamil serial has, 23 years later, become something that reminds me of home, my father, my childhood and the Malaysia I left behind.
I may be far from home, but my heart is there tonight. And I thank Petronas, one of our national prides, for sharing it again.
It brought a little Deepavali cheer to a Malaysian spending yet another festive season away from home.
'Selamat Hari Deepavali' to everyone celebrating, including Malaysians who, like me, are spending the festival far away from home.
LOSHI RAJEN
Merseyside, England

d470c95746552efd: The challenge is not solely to declare new protected areas, but ensure they have effective management
Originally published on Global Voices
The stunning beauty of the Dominican Republic’s north coast at Los Haitises National Park. Photo by Jason Boldero on Flickr (CC BY 2.0).

When you think of the Dominican Republic, the first thing that might come to mind is paradise where sun, sand, and sea combine to offer unforgettable experiences to Dominican families and global travellers alike — but the country’s deep sea is also of critical importance.

Jonathan Delance, director of conservation of the National 30×30 Program of the Ministry of Environment and Natural Resources, says that Dominican marine ecosystems are one of the country’s “greatest natural and strategic riches” — diverse, highly connected, and fundamental to national life.

From an ecological standpoint, coral reefs, mangroves, seagrass beds, dunes, beaches, pelagic zones, and deep-sea ecosystems sustain biodiversity. From an economic and social standpoint, they are the foundation of tourism, fishing, and coastal protection.

Despite relevant research being conducted in the country, information remains limited. According to Delance, some of the available studies on Dominican deep waters have had a geophysical, geochemical, or geological focus, rather than an ecological one. This is largely because deep-sea research is expensive, complex, and requires specialised technology, such as remotely operated vehicles, acoustic equipment, deep-sea cameras, and highly specific taxonomic capabilities.

Precisely because of these limitations, for a long time the National System of Protected Areas lacked a clear representation of deep ecosystems and their underwater geomorphologies, a gap that began to close with the inclusion of the Beata Underwater Ridge as a conservation object within the Orlando Jorge Mera Marine Sanctuary, representing a relevant step forward for the country.

As part of the scientific basis for this process, Delance explains that the technical report on deep-sea fauna documented research between 900 and 4,200 metres deep, recording 1,855 biological observations and 3,294 organisms. One of the most interesting finds was 148 morphospecies, defined in the book Marine Biodiversity as a “group of specimens that can be distinguished from others on the basis of morphological characteristics,” including poriferans, cnidarians, echinoderms, chordates, arthropods, annelids, mollusks, and other yet undetermined organisms.

The pelagic fauna expedition conducted in 2024 covered 2,771 kilometres (1,722 miles) and identified six species of cetaceans, 15 species of birds, as well as sharks and turtle routes. Environmental DNA resulted in the identification of species — including more than 400 morphospecies — along the entire food chain, demonstrating the health and complexity of this space.

Despite these advances, Delance notes, important gaps persist: “We need more information on taxonomic identification at the species level, genetic connectivity, oceanographic dynamics, seasonal distribution, cumulative impacts, biogeography of deep species, and the response of these ecosystems to underwater disturbances, climate change, and other pressures.”
What is deep-sea mining?

According to the International Seabed Authority (ISA), deep-sea mining (DSM) refers to the extraction of mineral resources from deposits located on the deep seabed, typically found between 400 metres (1.300 feet) and 6.5 kilometres (4 miles) beneath the ocean’s surface.

There are three primary types of mineral deposits. Polymetallic nodules (PMN) were discovered on March 7, 1873, during the Challenger expedition; scientists described them as “several peculiar black oval bodies which were composed of almost pure manganese oxide.” The ISA states that they are composed of manganese, iron, silicates, and hydroxides, and can be as small as micro-nodules or as large as 20 centimetres. They are commonly found on the west coast of Mexico in the Pacific Ocean (also known as the Clarion-Clipperton Fracture Zone), as well as the Central Indian Ocean Basin, and the Peru Basin. While polymetallic nodules can be found in lakes, the ones with greater economic value are typically located at depths of 4,000–6,000 metres (2.5 miles–3.7 miles), in areas with an extremely low sedimentation rate.

Polymetallic sulphides (PMS), which contain large amounts of copper, zinc, lead, iron, silver and gold, were first discovered in 1948 as part of the Swedish Albatross oceanographic expedition in the Red Sea. Later, in 1963 and 1966, scientists also found metalliferous muds and brines in the Red Sea Rift System.

Finally, cobalt-rich ferromanganese crusts (CFC) are found at depths of less than 400 metres (1.300 feet) to more than 5,000 metres (3 miles), mainly in areas with strong volcanic activity. While similar to polymetallic nodules in their composition, these crusts are attracting interest from mining companies because they can contain relatively high amounts of cobalt, as well as platinum, rare earth elements, nickel, and manganese.
The ISA has signed 15-year contracts with 22 contractors for DSM exploration, with most of them covering PMN, eight going to PMS and five to CFC.

The contractors range from national governments — including South Korea, India, Poland and Russia — to research institutes and private companies. A small number, such as South Korea, India and China’s Ocean Mineral Resources Research and Development Association, hold contracts across more than one deposit type, while the majority have a single contract.
The Dominican Republic’s position

The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), which opened for signature in Montego Bay, Jamaica, in 1982 and entered into force in 1994, establishes the overarching legal framework governing ocean space, marine scientific research and environmental protection.

A central component of the Convention is the definition of “the Area,” the seabed and ocean floor beyond the limits of national jurisdiction. UNCLOS declares the Area and its resources to be the “common heritage of mankind,” and establishes the ISA to administer these resources and regulate their exploration and eventual exploitation.
Between 2020 and 2025, the Dominican Republic had an active participation in the ISA, which is headquartered in Kingston, Jamaica.

At the ISA Assembly (ISBA28) in July 2023, Edward Pérez Reyes, the Dominican Republic’s then representative to the ISA, who twice served as its vice president, presented the country’s position on deep-sea mining. While he recognised the importance of these minerals for an energy transition, the DR advocated for a moratorium until there was a solid legal framework and sufficient scientific evidence to guarantee the protection of marine ecosystems. He also proposed sustainable alternatives, the circular economy, and recycling, as well as an equitable distribution of benefits and strengthening of the management of marine resources.

“The Dominican Republic was never against the International Seabed Authority or the process outlined by the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea,” Pérez Reyes, who is now the DR’s ambassador to Japan, explained. “Quite the opposite. We always understood that the international community’s effort to regulate the exploration and eventual exploitation of the seabed was a legitimate exercise. Before that legal framework existed, the risk was that countries with the technological capacity to do so would act on their own. The Convention came precisely to prevent that, and to establish common rules for everyone. So, the discussion was about something else. The question was whether the international community was already in a position to move from exploration to commercial exploitation. Our impression was that it was not yet.”

The DR’s stance, he said — the result of an inter-institutional process involving the Ministry of Environment and Natural Resources, the Ministry of Energy and Mines, the National Authority for Maritime Affairs (ANAMAR), and more — was never intended to halt the process. Rather, it was to allow science to keep advancing and for the ISA to finish building the regulatory framework that the Convention itself had mandated it to develop. “Every time we learned of a new research study,” Pérez Reyes recalled, “we ended up thinking that there was still much more to know. And that led us back to the same reflection: we had to continue researching before deciding such great consequence.”

Even today, the principles that guided that position still seem valid to him, though the information on which decisions are made can always change. “If science provides new elements, a responsible state has to analyse them,” Pérez Reyes added.

For Delance, scientific exploration of the deep sea is necessary to better understand these ecosystems before considering any form of utilisation. In his view, the DR still lacks key information, including biodiversity baselines, bathymetric and geomorphological maps, data on vulnerable species, ecological connectivity, oceanographic processes, environmental risks, and the resilience of ecosystems.

He believes that the Dominican stance in favour of a precautionary pause in deep-sea mining responds to the need to first generate sufficient scientific evidence to properly plan, regulate, and protect these spaces, and warned that if deep-sea ecosystems are not protected, the DR and wider Caribbean could lose still-unknown biodiversity, genetic resources of potential scientific value, migratory corridors, and essential habitats for threatened species. The country must therefore move, Delance believes, toward marine spatial planning in order to balance conservation and the sustainable use of these strategic ecosystems.
Environmental groups raise opposition

The Magua Ecological Foundation, which is committed to environmental conservation, biodiversity protection, and the sustainable use of natural resources, categorically disapproves of deep-sea mining in the DR, cautioning that the impacts could be severe and irreversible.

Its president, Manuel Alejandro Rodríguez, said that deep-sea mining represents a significant threat to marine ecosystems, whose biological richness and ecological value are fundamental to the well-being of present and future generations. DSM could lead to habitat destruction, species loss, pollution, and disruption of ecological processes, and potentially cause irreversible environmental damage due to the release of metals and other polluting substances into the marine environment.

“In an island nation like the Dominican Republic,” he stressed, “whose seas support extraordinary biodiversity and are essential for activities such as fishing, tourism, scientific research, and the protection of coastal communities, the risks associated with deep-sea mining far outweigh any potential economic benefits.”

Reaffirming the precautionary principle as a fundamental pillar of environmental management, he added, “As long as scientific uncertainties persist regarding the consequences of this activity and there are no guarantees that it can be carried out without causing irreparable damage, it is essential to prioritise the conservation of our marine ecosystems.”

The Foundation wants the authorities, the private sector, scientific community, and society in general to strengthen the protection of our oceans, promote public policies based on the best available scientific evidence, and commit to sustainable development models.

Sixto Inchaustegui, president of Grupo Jaragua, another NGO working for the sustainable management of biodiversity, said that the DR does not know where deep-sea mining activities could take place along its coasts, especially since its continental shelf is very narrow and the country relies heavily on marine and coastal ecosystem services, including tourism, fisheries, and protection against hurricanes. Such ecosystems are already highly threatened and degraded due to land-use changes, mangrove loss, erosion, overfishing, coral mortality, pollution, and other pressures, all of which are being exacerbated by climate change.
New representative to the ISA

On July 14, Ambassador Nancy Patricia Franjul Pérez presented her credentials as the DR’s new permanent representative to the ISA, and reaffirmed the country’s commitment to help develop a solid, transparent, and science-based regulatory framework for the exploitation of mineral resources in the Area.

Franjul Pérez also emphasised the critical role of the ISA at a time when the international community seeks to balance resource security, marine environmental protection, technological development, and the equitable distribution of benefits. ISA Secretary-General Leticia Carvalho said she looks forward to continuing the dialogue, “including on the draft exploitation regulations and the wider work of the Authority, in a spirit of transparency, environmental responsibility, and respect” for the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea.
The future of Dominican marine protection

In 2024, the DR became the first Caribbean country to surpass one of the targets of the global 30×30 environmental commitment, protecting 30.8 percent of its waters. As Delance explained, however, the challenge now is not solely to declare new protected areas, but to ensure they have effective management.

Currently, more than 90 percent of the protected marine area has management plans, a fundamental tool to guide conservation, regulate permitted uses, monitor ecosystems, and support decision-making. Looking to the future, efforts must focus on moving toward effective protection by strengthening monitoring and technological surveillance, regulating maritime traffic, developing national scientific capacity, and generating more research on deep ecosystems.

The DR will participate alongside Colombia in a scientific mission belonging to the inaugural programme of the REV Ocean, the world’s largest ocean research vessel, which will conduct the Beata Ridge mission in 2027.

The expedition will allow for the study of the deep ecosystems of the Beata Underwater Ridge, generate information on its biodiversity and ecological connectivity, and assess potential threats to strengthen ocean conservation and management. The country will also initiate a marine spatial planning process covering both protected and unprotected areas, enabling better organisation of ocean uses and supporting evidence-based decision-making.

6de4ffe311d20d73: KUALA LUMPUR: The man arrested with more than 100kg of syabu at the Brunei-Miri border in Sarawak on Oct 31 was a Malaysian believed to be travelling to Sabah.
Federal Narcotics Crime Investigation Department director Datuk Hussein Omar Khan said the 46-year-old suspect was from Miri, Sarawak, and had two previous criminal records.
"Police received information from Brunei's Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB) regarding the arrest of a Malaysian man by Brunei Customs at the Sungai Tujoh Control Post.
"Preliminary investigations based on information from the NCB found that the suspect was arrested while entering Brunei from Miri, Sarawak," he said when contacted.
Hussein said information from the Brunei authorities indicated that the suspect was believed to have used the country as a transit route before re-entering Malaysia.
"The suspect was expected to travel through Kuala Belait, Seria, Tutong and Bandar Seri Begawan before heading to Temburong via the Sultan Haji Omar 'Ali Saifuddien Bridge.
"He was then expected to re-enter Sarawak through Labu-Mengkalap before heading to Sabah via the Merapok-Sindumin route," he said.
He said the seized drugs, believed to be syabu, weighed an estimated 100kg and were worth about RM5 million.
Hussein said the department would continue intelligence cooperation with the NCB to identify the source of the drugs and possible links to syndicate networks in Malaysia.
"The department will continue intelligence coordination and cooperation with the NCB to obtain information on the source of the drugs.
"This cooperation is also aimed at identifying the possible involvement of individuals or drug trafficking syndicate networks linked to Malaysia," he said.
Earlier, Brunei authorities reported the seizure of 102.19kg of syabu concealed in 100 tea packets at the Sungai Tujoh Control Post along the Brunei-Miri border.
The drugs were estimated to be worth at least BND2.8 million, making it the largest drug seizure recorded at the control post.
Besides syabu, Brunei authorities also seized four Erimin 5 pills, RM1,180, S$10, BND10 and 500 baht in cash, two mobile phones and a vehicle believed to have been used in the operation.

57631f5dee3e81d6: LABUAN: The institute of logistics professionals has called for a comprehensive assessment to be carried out on the future of Kota Kinabalu International Airport to determine whether to retain, expand or relocate the airport.

Daniel Doughty, the Sabah chairman of the Chartered Institute of Logistics and Transport Malaysia, said decisions on the state's principal aviation gateway should be based on reliable evidence and balanced assessments rather than predetermined positions.

In a statement following a public forum on the future of KKIA held in Kota Kinabalu yesterday, he said: "Our responsibility isn't to tell the public what to think, but to provide the information that will allow the public to form better judgement."

Doughty said any decision whether to retain or relocate KKIA required rigorous evaluation, taking into account development costs, financing requirements, environmental impact and long-term economic implications.
The forum featured aviation consultant Edward Clayton and former civil aviation regulator Chester Voo, who shared their perspectives on KKIA's future development.

Doughty said expanding airport facilities alone would not guarantee more airlines or establish a successful aviation hub, as passenger demand, airline profitability and supporting industries were equally important.

The institute welcomed the state government's plan to undertake an integrated transport and logistics master plan study in 2027, covering air, land and maritime connectivity. It said airport development should be assessed as part of a wider transport and logistics strategy to ensure infrastructure investments deliver tangible economic benefits.
