Today, Thirunavukkarasan, assisted by his wife and children, sells a variety of traditional Indian food four times a week at several locations, including Putrajaya, Jalan Tuanku Abdul Rahman and TTDI.
Ever popular with customers, especially among the Malay community, some of his offerings include vadey, chapati, thosai, apam lenggang and murukku.
The father of three said his business flourished because his prices are affordable without compromising on quality. They are also halal-certified.
UMBI Project boost
On his participation in the UMBI Project, the Kuala Lumpur-born entrepreneur said his business received more attention after he joined the initiative last year.

The UMBI Project is a three-year initiative implemented by the Institute of Malaysian and International Studies (IKMAS), Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia (UKM), with the support of The Coca-Cola Foundation. It aims to help micro-entrepreneurs strengthen their business management foundations to build stable and consistent incomes.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Traditional Indian dishes, including ‘vadey’, ‘thosai’ and ‘chapati’, are among the offerings at Thirunavukkarasan Krishnana’s family-run food business. — Bernama pic
Thirunavukkarasan said he learned how to obtain halal certification, prepare halal food and what halal means via the UMBI Project.

“Through the project, my business gained greater exposure as the initiative brought customers from all over Malaysia, including those who were previously unfamiliar with my products, to make purchases. Sales rose,” he said.
Thirunavukkarasan hopes to pass on the family business to his children. But he said he has to ensure that they have the necessary know-how, coupled with education.
“I always remind them that if they find it difficult to secure a job after graduating from university, they are always welcome to continue the family business legacy,” he said.
In conjunction with the Deepavali celebrations, Thirunavukkarasan’s story reflects his love, sacrifice and his spirit of perseverance.

These are the foundations to preserve his heritage and family legacy. Together with his traditional halal food offerings, he continues to build a legacy enjoyed and cherished by a multi-racial community. — Bernama
5eba23d5c4101fa6: BATAM, Nov 8 — Cooking and bathing became difficult when taps ran dry in Batam, an Indonesian island where residents are protesting as data centres spring up to power the global artificial intelligence boom.
The area had suffered a “long drought” caused by low rainfall, the local water utility operator told AFP, as a strong El Nino cycle exacerbates dry weather.

But, as in other countries, anger has been directed at the data centres, warehouse-like facilities that keep apps and artificial intelligence tools running, with water often used to cool their humming servers.
Frustration is bubbling over in Indonesia and Malaysia — especially in regions bordering Singapore that are seen as a prime location for new tech facilities.
At first the main reaction was, “thank God industry is coming” to Batam, 54-year-old tradesman Juniardi Adinda Sembiring Gurukinayan told AFP.
But severe recent outages hitting the municipal water service in some Batam communities meant “sometimes I skipped my shower”.
“We cannot eat rice without water. We cannot cook vegetables without water,” he said.
At the worst point, dozens of angry residents staged spontaneous protests outside Nongsa Digital Park — a new cluster of data centres and other amenities, designated a special economic zone.
People in the district believe “that the water shortages... are related to the construction of data centres”, Juniardi said.

The drought caused the nearby Nongsa Reservoir to run very low, and supply systems were further disrupted by an electrical fault, said Ginda Alamsyah, a spokesman for water utility operator Air Batam Hilir (ABH).
The tech park receives water from a different source, Duriangkang Reservoir, an industry source told AFP.
‘Smelly, yellowish’
Authorities in late September told developers they must build plants to desalinate seawater for cooling, to avoid straining local resources.
Companies behind operational or planned data centres at Nongsa Digital Park include the Singapore-headquartered BW Digital, DayOne, and Princeton Digital Group.
Another owner, Hong Kong-based Gaw Capital Partners, said it was “aware of the distress and frustration expressed by local residents in Nongsa and surrounding Batam communities” over water shortages.
To ensure sustainable operations, “our data centre facilities must deploy a combination of advanced engineering, efficient architectural designs, and renewable energy sourcing,” it said.
That includes using so-called “closed-loop” water systems that reuse resources and so require less fresh liquid.
As residents demanded a return to normal water supply at one protest last month, AFP saw a police officer filling up buckets they had brought to Nongsa Digital Park.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

This aerial picture shows the Nongsa Digital Park (NDP) area, a hub for artificial intelligence (AI)-based data centre and digital infrastructure development, in Batam, Riau Islands, November 3, 2026. — AFP pic
In nearby coastal village Mata Ikan, people had to use seawater to wash after defecating, said demonstrator Rahmat, 52, who like many Indonesians goes by one name.

“The water crisis has been going on for the past year, but it got worse in the last six months,” 38-year-old Sulastri said at her home, where supply was out, so she poured water from a plastic bottle to wash dishes.
“Many of us here run small stalls. We used to make ice cubes, but we can’t anymore.”
The government has been distributing water from tanks driven around, but Sulastri said it was “smelly” and “yellowish”.
AFP contacted the local government BP Batam, and Indonesia’s ministry for economic affairs, which regulates Nongsa Digital Park, for comment. Neither responded.

Recent disruption to water distribution “was not caused by data centres or AI or investors entering that sector,” Amsakar Achmad, Batam mayor and head of BP Batam said in October, according to local media.
The decline in water supply was instead “due to weather and climate factors”, he said.
Tech boom
Data centre capacity in South-east Asia is projected to triple from 2025 levels by 2030, driven by a tenfold surge in AI use, according to a KPMG report.
This can put pressure on water supplies, but also electricity grids still heavily reliant on planet-warming fossil fuels.
The data centre construction boom in Indonesia and Malaysia began when resource constraints led hyper-connected Singapore to halt new developments between 2019 and 2022.
It has since ramped up, boosting both countries’ economies as governments and tech giants pour hundreds of billions of dollars into training and running AI.
Ginda said water provider ABH supports policies to encourage investment and development in Batam, south of Singapore and connected to it by undersea cables.
But he added that water demand must be managed properly, adding that ABH is trying to boost the capacity of Batam’s six reservoirs by dredging them, with cloud seeding another option in dry periods.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Residents extend a supply hose to fill a barrel with clean water from a tanker truck in Kavling Bakau Serip, amid local water shortages linked to the intensive water requirements of the growing artificial intelligence (AI) data centre developments at Nongsa Digital Park in Batam, Riau Islands, November 3, 2026. — AFP pic
‘Inflection point’
North of Singapore, Malaysia’s Johor region has become “one of the largest emerging AI infrastructure clusters in the world”, according to researcher James Chai of the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute.
Just half a decade ago, Johor hosted 10 megawatts of data centre capacity. That has ballooned by a factor of 200 to 2.1 gigawatts today, Chai said.
The environmental cost could be high.
By 2035, data centres are forecast to swallow up one-third of Malaysia’s total energy consumption, the deputy prime minister told parliament in July.
The government said at that time it would only approve data centre projects after ensuring sufficient energy and water supply capacity.
Johor residents have protested over dust pollution and flash floods linked to data centre construction, as operators build closer to residential areas.
“Johor is at a critical inflection point,” Mohd Fadhil Md Din of Malaysia’s University of Technology told AFP.
“It has the potential to become South-east Asia’s leading sustainable data centre hub,” but only if it manages resources and spatial planning carefully, he said.
‘We all feel it’
Pushback sometimes works.
In Kota Damansara on the outskirts of Kuala Lumpur, a plot of land intended for a data centre remains empty after local opposition.
The developer withdrew its planning permission application in August, after its neighbours spoke out online, lobbied their MP and gathered more than 9,000 petition signatures.
Jahaidi Harun, 72, had been concerned that the proposed data centre could be noisy and pressure existing infrastructure.
Data centres “use a lot of water,” the retiree told AFP, adding that, as in Batam, “if the rain doesn’t come for one month, we all feel it”.
Following the withdrawal, Malaysia’s human resources minister Ramanan Ramakrishnan told local media he wasn’t against “development or investment”.
But “for large-scale projects that could affect the residents’ lives, the people must have a say”. — AFP
79bae9b71c9a01b9: NEW YORK, Nov 8 — Airlines are installing deluxe seats, enlisting Michelin-star chefs for luxury menu offerings and designing elite airport lounges as the industry bets its future on growing demand for premium travel.

The strategy is expected to accelerate the shrinking share of coach class on many flights, with airlines envisioning as much as 70 per cent of passengers paying for enhanced options, if not first-or business class.
Airlines face significantly higher jet fuel costs due to the Iran war, but view such upselling as a profitable long-term bet.

Business class seats can each take up floor space equivalent to four basic-level seats, but can be priced five or six times higher, said Volodymyr Bilotka, a professor at Purdue University and a specialist in aviation economics.
“Airlines have traditionally been investing quite a lot into the premium offerings because the profit margins are significantly higher,” Bilotka told AFP.

In the most recent quarter, American Airlines said premium revenue increased 18.5 per cent year-over-year, four points better than the main cabin. The boost has been a bright spot in a travel market complicated by the jet fuel spike, American executives said.
“Premium products generate roughly half of the company’s ticket revenue on approximately 30 per cent of seats today,” American said.

Besides the traditional differentiation between the main cabin and business class, customers may now pay as much as $200 for more legroom or the ability to sit at the front of the plane and disembark first.
United Airlines announced in July that it would offer a new Economy Plus option that allows customers to forgo having a passenger in the dreaded middle seat.
United plans to begin this option on some flights at the end of 2026.
In September, JetBlue announced the launch of BlueFirst, a new first-class service on domestic flights.
“Customers are increasingly looking for more premium experiences,” said JetBlue CEO Joanna Geraghty.
Premium’s steady growth
Since 2020, the number of premium seats on US flights has risen 33 per cent, more than double the growth of mainline seats, according to travel news site Skift.
United Airlines more than doubled its premium-seat capacity between 2015 and 2026, the airline told AFP, adding that it plans additional options, like seats with extra elbow room.
Delta has invested in DeltaOne, a revamped luxury option, with premium wine, “top-of-the line” food like the Wagyu burger and larger screens for entertainment.
To assist with the menu, Delta partnered with Simon Hulstone, chef of a Michelin-star restaurant in Britain, and Andrea Robinson, an award-winning sommelier.
The company plans the service for new Airbus A350 planes, with about 150 premium seats and 161 seats in economy.

“Twenty years ago, 90 per cent of the seats were main cabin,” said Ekrem Dimbiloglu, Delta’s managing director for onboard strategy and experience, adding that the share of premium seats could soon represent as much as 70 per cent on some Delta flights.
No major carrier has so far launched service without any economy seats.
In October, British Airways announced that the top level of the two-tier A380 would be entirely composed of premium seats.

Consultancy Cirium estimates that premium seats among the 42 carriers in the three major airline alliances (SkyTeam, Oneworld and Star Alliance) and Middle East carriers now represent 19 per cent of total volume compared with 17.1 per cent in 2019.

Other new options include giving customers choice among meal options prior to boarding and free Wi-Fi. There have also been a slew of announcements of new and beautified airport lounges, including by Southwest Airlines, which was once known as a discount carrier.

But the increasing tendency of airlines to market to customers who can afford premium amenities could open the door to a discount carrier, although higher fuel costs have added to the challenges facing all airlines. — AFP
ca674e1f43a3d039: WELLINGTON, Nov 8 — New Zealand’s political future hangs in the balance after a knife-edge vote that produced no clear winner.
Preliminary results show Prime Minister Christopher Luxon’s right-wing coalition holds the balance of power, with only a narrow path to victory for the left-wing opposition.
Here’s what happens now the election is over.
What votes are left to count?
Preliminary results released by New Zealand’s electoral commission early this morning showed a tally of 2.4 million votes cast during the advance period and on election day.

They do not include nearly 400,000 so-called “special votes”, among them around 100,000 votes cast overseas and those cast by people within New Zealand but outside the local electorate in which they live.
The full and final tally of votes will be released on November 27.
Historically, special votes leaned left, giving the Labour Party or Green Party an additional one or two seats in parliament at the expense of the right-bloc.
That can be either through changes to the total party vote, or through changes in the closest local electorate seats.
Overhangover
Under the Mixed-Member Proportional (MMP) system, New Zealanders cast two votes — one for their local electorate representative and one for the party they wish to govern.
The 71 electorate members advance directly into parliament, with the remaining members decided based on party vote per centages.
For example, the Labour Party received 29.36 per cent of the preliminary vote, which gave it 36 seats.
Because it won 21 electorate races, those members are directly elected to represent the party and the remaining 15 members are assigned based on their ranking on the party list.
The system is designed to give parties that meet a five per cent voter threshold proportional power in parliament.
But this year, voters have manipulated the system by engineering a so-called “overhang”, whereby a party secures more local electorate seats than their vote per centage would normally allow.
The National Party has received 29.21 per cent of votes, which entitles it to 36 seats in the House.
But the party has won 42 local electorate races, meaning it received six seats more than it would otherwise be entitled to.
The left-wing indigenous Te Pati Maori also secured five electorate seats when its party vote was less than one per cent, a five-seat overhang.
It means parliament swells to its largest ever size on preliminary voting with 131 members, who may not even fit into the already-cramped debating chamber in Wellington.
Seat flipping
All eyes now will be on a select few tight electorate races which could flip the election to the left-bloc, but their path to victory remains very narrow.
Labour Party candidates trail by margins of just a few hundred in two key races: Hamilton East and Wairarapa.
There are other seats National could flip in its favour based on special votes, however.
If Labour flipped those two seats and retained wins in other tight races, it would reduce National’s majority and the size of parliament, but the right-bloc would still cling to power.
The Labour-led opposition also needs a significant change in both electorates and party voting in order to clinch victory, but National’s overhang insulates it from any party voting changes.
Coalition talks
With the final votes in on November 27, only then will the parties begin coalition negotiations to form the next government.
But if the six-week-long talks that followed the last election are any hint, an official arrangement may not be in place this year.
The current coalition of National, libertarian ACT and populist NZ First have been in an uneasy alliance since 2023 and have said that they will work with each other again.
If the left-bloc breaks through in special voting, it could form a four-headed coalition with the Green Party, Te Pati Maori, and centrist newcomers Opportunity.
Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong has said her party will first negotiate with the party with the most votes. — AFP
ae883b93a76a8889: ISTANBUL, Nov 8 — As the COP31 climate summit approaches, host nation Turkey is putting electrification front and centre, touting its renewables boom while pushing its Zero Waste agenda as a way to reduce methane emissions.

But local environmental campaigners say it sidesteps the “elephant in the room” of Turkey’s ongoing reliance on coal and obscures the fact it has effectively become “Europe’s dumping ground” for plastic waste.

When the UN summit opens tomorrow in Antalya, COP31 President Murat Kurum, who is also Turkey’s environment minister, will be pushing Ankara’s flagship initiative to make electricity account for 35 per cent of global energy demand by 2035.
The non-binding “35 by 35” target is key to a 10-point Action Agenda that Turkey says will speed up the shift to renewables while shoring up energy security.

“This year’s energy crisis has shocked us ... everyone now understands that energy that you import is energy that you do not control. Electrification is the answer. It protects communities from volatile global markets and cuts emissions,” Kurum said on Thursday.
COP31’s aim is “to usher in the age of electricity”, he said.
Renewable energy drive

Turkey has made huge advances in renewables infrastructure in recent years, with Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar on Thursday unveiling an ambitious US$500 billion (RM2 trillion) roadmap to electrify its economy and expand its installed wind and solar capacity fourfold to 175 gigawatts.

Yet with a third of its electricity derived from coal, no date for phasing it out and plans to expand two existing coal-fired power plants alongside its electrification drive, COP31 will be a test for Turkey’s climate leadership, campaigners say.
“What electrification should do is end the dependency on fossil fuels. That should be the ultimate goal,” said Emel Turker Alpay, an energy campaigner with Greenpeace Turkey.
She warned the “35 by 35” target did not specify electricity should be generated by clean energy — the only way to deliver climate benefits.
“The most important thing would be a commitment to no new coal in Turkey and giving a date for starting a just transition away from fossil fuels,” she told AFP.

Unlike last year’s host Brazil, which put emissions reductions at the heart of its COP agenda, Turkey has largely avoided debate over fossil fuel phase-out, with Bayraktar saying an exit from coal would depend on Turkey ramping up its nuclear power production.
Turkey’s first nuclear plant is due to come online by the year’s end, with plans to set up two more.
‘Weak’ climate targets

Both Turkey and COP31 co-host Australia, which is steering the negotiations, have set targets for reducing heat-trapping emissions, but neither has adopted a national “roadmap” explicitly detailing plans to exit fossil fuels.
Although Turkey has set a net-zero goal of 2053, Climate Action Tracker last month warned its interim targets fell short, with its overall rating still “critically insufficient”.

“Turkey ... faces a crisis of contradiction: while calling for accelerated climate action, its own targets are weak and lack the ambition necessary to drive much-needed emissions reductions,” it said, urging Ankara to “strengthen” its 2030 and 2035 targets.
Yagiz Eren Abanus of the Centre for Spatial Justice — one of 17 environmental organisations in the Turkish Climate Network — said the country’s targets needed a radical rethink.

“Turkey is not decreasing greenhouse gases but increasing them,” he explained, saying that despite Ankara’s pledge to cut projected emissions by 41 per cent by 2035, in real terms it allows “a 16-per cent increase” from today’s levels.
Plastic waste

Turkey is also championing its Zero Waste Initiative, a high-profile environmental diplomacy campaign led by Emine Erdogan, wife of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, seeking to push international cooperation to reduce methane emissions from waste.
“When you look at the Action Agenda, they want to reduce projected global waste growth by 50 per cent by 2035, which is a good thing,” said Greenpeace’s Alpay.

“But these policies are only focusing on managing waste after it is produced, and not preventing waste at its source. Without stronger commitments to waste prevention and methane reduction, it won’t deliver meaningful emission cuts,” she told AFP.
Turkey has not endorsed the Global Methane Pledge and is still importing plastic waste, notably from Europe, which is closely linked to emissions.

“The plastics industry is the fossil fuel industry’s Trojan horse because when they cannot use the fuels they extracted for energy production, they redirect it into the petrochemical industry,” Alpay explained.
“When we limit waste management to recycling, it doesn’t mean much for climate change or emissions.” — AFP
08b99c2359fc2086: KARACHI, Nov 8 — Wheeling its way between dining booths at a neon-lit restaurant in Pakistan’s Karachi megacity, a robot waitress drops off a fresh pizza to an awaiting family.
While global buzz is growing around agile humanoids made in the United States, China and elsewhere, robotic staff are a rare sight in the South Asian country.
“Welcome to Sicilian. My name is Robia,” the waitress says in an electronic voice, looking down at diners through blinking red LED eyes.
Robia and her colleague Jojo are the DIY creations of Pakistani engineer Syed Osama Aziz, who is bringing a sci-fi reboot to Karachi’s storied dining scene.
They have spherical white heads and dark visors, similar to a motorcycle helmet, and sport black shawls around their neck in the style of a dupatta worn by women in the region.
Aziz, who also established The Sicilian restaurant, developed the machines using mostly locally manufactured parts, designing their circuit boards and programming them in his own lab.
“The equipment, the things needed to make robots, are not so easily available here, so we had to arrange them,” he told AFP.
The duo were developed through his robotics company, Cobot, with help from friends and some electronic components imported from abroad.

In China and other East Asian countries especially, robots are an increasingly common sight, shuttling food to customers in chain restaurants and taking on other jobs from cleaning to greeting hotel guests.
But they remain a novelty in Pakistan, where Aziz’s home-grown creations are attracting curious diners.
When they arrive at a table, the customers must either take the food off their serving tray themselves or wait for a human member of staff to assist them.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Pakistani engineer and founder of The Sicilian restaurant, Syed Osama Aziz, developed two robot waitresses using mostly locally manufactured components for his restaurant in Karachi. — AFP pic
Excited customers
Aziz, whose workshop manufacturing the robots is located in Multan in Pakistan’s central Punjab province, hopes to make his creations more sophisticated in the future.
“Our plans are to add camera-based processing and image-processing features,” he said.
“That means the robot will also recognise you by looking at you, and it will remember what you ordered last time, and accordingly it will be able to give you better suggestions.”
For now, the robots are proving a hit with families, who flock to the restaurant to watch the machines in action.
“The best thing about it is that it introduces itself,” excited customer Ahmer Zameer told AFP, explaining the robot also “tells you what things you can order”.
Children reach out to touch the robots while their parents snap photographs and selfies.
Young customer Sonia Dilosker said she was impressed by the androids’ appearance and preferred their approach to serving customers, “because it is a machine and without any emotions”.
Restaurant staff say the novelty has brought a surge in customers — some travelling from across the sprawling port city to meet the robots.
“Our business has grown. People are coming from far away for this. They have seen a robot for the first time here,” staff member Hellen told AFP.
“People are excited to see this.” — AFP

bc4d6388f11051bf: WASHINGTON: Nasa has announced that it is developing a rover named PROMISE, which is scheduled to land near the Moon’s South Pole in 2028, reported Sputnik/RIA Novosti.
“Nasa announced it is moving forward with the development of PROMISE (Polar Rover for Observation, Mapping, and In-Situ Exploration).

“Equipped with scientific instruments and technology demonstrations, the six-wheeled rover will land at the Moon’s South Pole. Nasa is targeting late 2028 for the launch of PROMISE,” the statement read.
The PROMISE rover will carry a drill to extract lunar regolith for analysis of ice and other resources on the Moon, Nasa said.

7ffa67322f49a6d8: MELAKA: The electoral alliance of Barisan Nasional and Perikatan Nasional in the Melaka state election does not guarantee a full transfer of votes between their supporters, state Pakatan Harapan chairman Adly Zahari said today.
He said supporters of the two coalitions might not all embrace the alliance, while new voters could also influence the election outcome.
In previous elections, some voters had chosen PN because they did not want to support BN, and the cooperation could therefore affect their existing support base. "The same applies to BN," he said.
He said the highest vote transfer rate recorded in the recent Negeri Sembilan state election was 70% to BN.

"The remaining 30% of BN votes might not go to PN. In Melaka, however, the rate could be 60% or even 50%, depending on how their supporters respond to the cooperation," he said while campaigning for re-election in Bukit Katil for a third term.

Adly, a former Melaka chief minister, said there were nearly 4,000 new voters in Bukit Katil whose presence could also influence voting patterns, as most had no strong allegiance to any political party.

He said Bukit Katil is a mixed constituency, with Malays accounting for about 65% of voters, followed by Chinese (29%) and Indians (5%). However, playing on racial and religious sentiments did not guarantee support, as loyalties were divided among several political parties.
"In the previous state election, Malay support for PH exceeded 27%, and we will try to increase that figure," he said.

Adly is challenged by Ridzuan Sarif of PN, Aliza Che Amran (Bersama) and Abu Bakar Sabudin (Independent) in a four-cornered contest for the seat. In the 2021 election, Adly retained the seat with a majority of 1,057 votes.
Early voting takes place on Nov 10, with polling on Nov 14.
85834917829515b1: PETALING JAYA: The Terengganu government will give a Chinese leader from Gerakan a position as an appointed assemblyman to ensure the community is represented in the state legislature, says menteri besar Ahmad Samsuri Mokhtar.
He said the state constitution allows the appointment of assemblymen from ethnic groups or genders unrepresented in the state assembly.

“We made the decision, after considering several matters, to appoint a Chinese (community representative) from Gerakan as an appointed assemblyman. I hope this is good news for all,” he said in a statement today.
Samsuri expressed hope that the representative would help the state government engage with the state’s various communities.

d0ebe560a9f13508: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 8 — Independent bookshop Lit Books is leaving its original Tropicana Avenue home in Petaling Jaya after nine years, relocating to downtown Kuala Lumpur early next year amid declining foot traffic.

In a statement shared on The Lit Books Blog, co-founder Fong Min Hun said the commercial landscape around the Petaling Jaya premises had changed considerably since the bookshop opened in December 2017.
“While we could probably chug along for a while longer, we have seen a steady decline in footfall over the past few years — a trend that is unlikely to reverse course anytime soon,” he said.
Fong said leaving the original premises was an emotional decision for him and his wife, Elaine Lau, with whom he founded the independent bookshop.
“Closing a chapter on the space that made us who we are is not easy, and no one feels the weight of that decision more than Elaine and myself.”
The move will take Lit Books into central Kuala Lumpur, drawn by the area’s foot traffic, energy and history.
Beyond the commercial considerations, however, Fong said the relocation also held personal significance.
Recalling his childhood, he described exploring Chinatown and Bukit Bintang with his best friend during an era of minibuses, arcade parlours and cinemas such as the Odeon and Rex.
Those experiences left a lasting impression, making the prospect of opening a bookshop in one of the spaces he once frequented particularly appealing.
“And so when the opportunity arose for us to actually set up shop in one of those very spaces, well, it was a no-brainer,” he wrote.
Fong did not disclose the exact location of the new premises, saying details of its final trading days at Tropicana Avenue and the downtown opening would be announced soon.
Founded by the husband-and-wife team of former journalists in 2017, Lit Books has built a following for its carefully selected range of English-language fiction and nonfiction.
The bookshop has also established itself as a gathering place for the local literary community, hosting author appearances, book discussions and other events.
Its second branch, located within stationery retailer CzipLee at Bangsar Village 2 in Kuala Lumpur, will continue operating.
For Fong and Lau, the move marks the end of a formative chapter for the business and an opportunity to establish itself in a different part of the Klang Valley.
Thanking customers for their support over the years, Fong expressed optimism about what lay ahead.
“It’s been a brilliant ride thus far. I’m looking forward to the next leg.”
32ff9cd31f9e0aa8: LABUAN: A dance troupe from Labuan has won gold in the folklore category of the world dance festival held in Shah Alam, competing against 144 teams from 10 countries and territories.

The Labuan Youth Dansa team presented a creative interpretation of a traditional Brunei dance, blending authentic movements with modern choreography and contemporary ethnic elements while preserving its cultural identity.

The troupe, established by the Labuan youth council, made its international debut at the festival. The 13-member Labuan delegation comprised nine dancers, a team manager, a choreographer and three support crew members.
Youth council president Nazera Roslan said the victory demonstrated the ability, creativity and potential of talented young Labuans.
"Winning gold on our debut is proof that our local arts and cultural heritage have the appeal to be showcased on the world stage," she said.

Choreographer Dafi Chua said the success was the result of the team's commitment, discipline, and cooperation in combining traditional Brunei dance movements with modern elements without compromising its original identity.

Malaysia was represented by 40 entrants at the festival, the second-highest to the 47 entries from India. Other countries taking part were Mongolia (21), Indonesia (18), Qatar (six), South Korea (five), Russia (three), Hong Kong, China (two), and the Philippines and Singapore (one each).
94781899d7df285d: HONG KONG, Nov 8 — Philippines tennis trailblazer Alex Eala dissolved into tears as she reflected on a “life-changing” season after falling agonisingly short of a second WTA Tour title today.
The second seed was stunned 6-3, 6-0 by Claire Liu in the final of the Hong Kong Open as the American ranked 102 won her first tour title.
Eala is at a career-high 17 in the world after a breakout year in which the 21-year-old clinched her maiden title, in Washington DC, in August.
That victory made her the first player from the Philippines to win a tournament on the WTA Tour.
Eala, set to rise to 15 in the world next week, started the year ranked 50th.
“This season has changed my life, it’s changed my life for the better,” Eala, who finished the final with heavy strapping on her right leg, told the crowd afterwards.
Becoming emotional as she addressed her team in the stands, she said: “I’m incredibly proud of the work we’ve put in this year.

414b97ddee29fa7f: Superconductors carry electricity without resistance, but most only work a few degrees above absolute zero. In the late 1980s, copper-based materials called cuprates were found to superconduct at higher temperatures—reachable with affordable liquid nitrogen. Yet nearly 40 years later, physicists still don't agree on why.

In a recent Science study, a team of physicists led by Milan Allan of Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich and Ingmar Swart of Utrecht University in the Netherlands has found some answers by listening to the faint electrical crackle of current flowing into a cuprate.

Central to the mystery of cuprates’ high-temperature superconductivity is a strange state called the pseudogap. “The pseudogap is a phenomenon of missing electrons,” Allan said. Above the temperature at which cuprates become superconducting, some of their electrons seem to vanish—measurements find far fewer of them at the energies where they should be. “Everybody knows that from different probes, you see that there's these vanishing electrons, but nobody knows why,” Allan said.

e07d7fb4d3ab3cb4: SINGAPORE, Nov 8 — Love munching on iced gem biscuits or other old-school snacks during your childhood?
For those looking to relive the nostalgia, traditional tidbit shop Biscuit King at Upper Thomson is one place you can still find these goodies. But not for much longer.
Biscuit King is set to close on January 31, 2027.
The store’s handwritten closure notice was shared by Patricia Chew in Facebook group Can Eat! SG yesterday.
“We regret to inform you that Biscuit King will be ceasing operations in a few months’ time,” it wrote.
“From the bottom of our hearts, thank you for your loyalty, support and wonderful memories over the years. It has been a true privilege serving you.”
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A handwritten notice at Biscuit King announces that the Singapore snack shop will cease operations on January 31, 2027. — Picture via Facebook/PatriciaChew
According to Biscuit King’s owner Benny Ong, the closure was due to a few main factors.
“Firstly, the cost of biscuits has increased over the years,” he told The Straits Times, adding that the latest hike only happened recently.
On top of that, Benny’s supplier had also projected an increase of more than 30 per cent in the cost of plastic bags and containers this year.
The shop could also face higher rental costs, as its current landlord is selling the property.
There are no plans to relocate or move the business online, Benny said.
News of Biscuit King’s impending closure drew attention from netizens.

One recalled visiting the store during their school days, writing: “We would drop by to buy stuff from that shop and I remember the owner used to wear a white singlet, long brown pants and the wife a traditional cheongsam top.”
“Sad. I love this place. Loved the variety and nostalgic biscuits. Brings back childhood memories. I’ve got to stock up,” said another.
Biscuit King started out in 1982 as a provision shop named Chua Seng Minimart.
It was subsequently registered under its current name in 2008.
The store sells old-school snacks such as iced gem biscuits, butterfly crackers and lemon puffs, among others.
Traditional sweets, toys and cards are also available here, including chocolate “goggles”, Old Maid playing cards and pick-up sticks.
A check on the snack shop’s website on Sunday showed that online orders are temporarily closed due to a shortage of manpower.
AsiaOne has reached out to Biscuit King for more information.
Address: 130 Casuarina Road, Singapore 579518
Opening hours: 11am to 10pm (Tuesday to Sunday) — AsiaOne

4df4e739dff7e703: Can an IBM Z mainframe run Doom? Of course it can. The more interesting question is whether you can play it through a text terminal without ruining your eyesight.

WND Software's browser demo connects to an IBM Z mainframe over SSH using its terminal emulator. Wojciech Graj's DOOM-ASCII supplies the text-based carnage, replacing conventional graphics with colored characters. There's no sound.

It is, however, completely playable (although you might need to recalibrate your vision to work out what is going on, particularly with regard to distant objects). Sessions are limited to five minutes, with room for up to 50 simultaneous users, but we had no trouble getting in. ASCII also presented no issues once the game was in motion. This writer played the original shareware release on an Amstrad ALT386SX portable, so squinting at an indistinct demon felt reassuringly familiar.

That Doom can be persuaded to run on an IBM Z mainframe is not particularly noteworthy. The code has turned up everywhere from databases to PCB designers. Even the humble Pi Pico was roped into the fun.

Keeping the action playable through a text terminal is the more entertaining achievement. A year ago, an IBM consultant persuaded Doom to run on IBM Z and LinuxONE using VNC to bring the pixelated mayhem to life. Using a terminal emulator, while a neat demonstration of the capabilities of WND's software, is perhaps more an example of "because I can" masochism.
It's undeniably an enjoyable way to burn through five minutes. No installation or login required – just a willingness to shoot at punctuation. ®
2e176eaacebb98da: DOHA, Nov 8 — Communications Minister Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil highlighted Malaysia’s progress in expanding its 5G network at Mobile World Congress (MWC) Doha 2026, with the country’s second 5G network achieving 90 per cent coverage in October this year, nine months ahead of schedule.

365904d718b8ed4c: DOHA, Nov 8 — Malaysia sees significant opportunities to leverage satellite connectivity and artificial intelligence (AI) to strengthen disaster preparedness and communications resilience, said Communications Minister Datuk Fahmi Fadzil.

Speaking at the Digital Leadership Forum Ministerial Panel held in conjunction with Mobile World Congress (MWC) Doha 2026 here today, he said emerging technologies could complement conventional telecommunications infrastructure, particularly in remote and disaster-affected areas where alternative connectivity solutions might be required.
He said Malaysia also saw potential in integrating terrestrial and non-terrestrial networks to strengthen communications resilience during emergencies.

“Looking ahead, Malaysia sees opportunities to further leverage emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, satellite connectivity and integrated terrestrial and non-terrestrial networks, to strengthen disaster preparedness and communications resilience.
“These technologies can complement conventional infrastructure, particularly in remote or disaster-affected areas where alternative connectivity solutions may be required,” he said.

Fahmi said Malaysia was placing greater emphasis on strengthening emergency telecommunications capabilities to ensure essential communications remained available when conventional networks were disrupted.
He said reliable connectivity was crucial during disasters as it enabled emergency response teams to coordinate rescue operations and affected communities to access essential information.
“During a disaster, connectivity is not merely a convenience. It can be the difference between receiving timely assistance and being left isolated,” he said.

To address these challenges, Fahmi said the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC) had developed MCMC PRIME, a mobile radio and internet communications system designed to support connectivity when conventional telecommunications networks are disrupted..
He said the system provided an alternative means of communication during emergencies and supported coordination among response teams while maintaining access to essential information.
He said the initiative was particularly relevant during severe flooding when damaged telecommunications infrastructure or disrupted electricity supply could affect conventional mobile networks.

Fahmi said Malaysia’s approach also emphasised close coordination between MCMC and telecommunications operators, as well as the National Disaster Management Agency (NADMA) and other relevant authorities.

He said such cooperation was essential to support disaster preparedness and identify affected network infrastructure while coordinating restoration efforts and facilitating communications for emergency responders and affected communities.
He also stressed the importance of timely public warnings and reliable access to official information to enable communities to take appropriate precautionary measures during emergencies.

“Network resilience is not simply about preventing infrastructure failure. It is about ensuring that essential communications can continue, or be restored as quickly as possible, when lives and public safety are at stake,” he said. — Bernama
06957ce02a0a71f7: DOHA, Nov 8— Malaysia has called for greater respect for national sovereignty in shaping telecommunications policies, warning against a form of “technology colonialism” in which technologically advanced nations dictate how other countries develop and deploy their digital infrastructure.

Communications Minister Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil said every nation must retain the freedom to determine its own technological direction, particularly as geopolitical rivalries and competing technology ecosystems increasingly influence global telecommunications development.
“There should not be a case of a kind of technology colonialism where if you are the first, then you dictate to others what you should or shouldn’t do, what you can or cannot do.
“Nations are sovereign and should be able to decide their own domestic policy,” he said during a ministerial panel discussion at Mobile World Congress (MWC) Doha 2026 here today.
Fahmi said Malaysia’s experience in rolling out its 5G network demonstrated the importance of maintaining policy independence while navigating complex geopolitical and diplomatic considerations.

He noted that Malaysia initially adopted a single wholesale network model for its 5G deployment despite recommendations against such an approach by GSMA Intelligence, before subsequently transitioning to a dual-network model.

“Malaysia is unique because we did what GSMA Intelligence said not to do: roll out 5G using a single wholesale network. But we did it anyway, and I was the minister in charge of transitioning it into a dual-network model,” he said.

Fahmi described the transition as a challenging undertaking that required Malaysia to navigate diplomatic sensitivities while balancing domestic priorities against international technological standards.
He stressed that discussions on digital sovereignty should extend beyond technological self-reliance to encompass the broader principle of national sovereignty.
The minister also said an increasingly multipolar global environment demands greater dialogue and engagement among countries to find common ground rather than deepen divisions.
“In this increasingly multipolar age, we need to have more conversations, more engagements, and find meeting points rather than things that split us apart,” he added.

Fahmi said the principle of interoperability, which enables different telecommunications networks and technologies to function together, would face significant tests as countries pursued their respective digital strategies.

He pointed out that ASEAN’s consensus-based approach presents its own unique dynamics, given the absence of a central parliament and the bloc’s strong emphasis on respecting member states’ national sovereignty.
As such, he said, building trust and achieving interoperability requires countries to look beyond their national borders and bolster international cooperation.
Fahmi also highlighted the need to assist emerging nations in bridging digital divides, particularly as the telecommunications sector prepares for quantum migration and quantum-safe communications.
He noted that greater focus should be placed on driving the practical adoption of existing networks before the industry shifts its attention entirely to sixth-generation (6G) technologies.
“Before we talk about 6G, we have to look at who is actually using 5G or 5G-Advanced - that remains a key challenge we are actively addressing in Malaysia,” he said.
Despite the hurdles, Fahmi expressed confidence that international collaboration could spur innovative breakthroughs, particularly from nations not traditionally viewed as global technology leaders.

“There are many challenges, but there are also many opportunities for us to discover solutions together, and sometimes you might find those solutions in the unlikeliest of countries,” he said. — Bernama

0bd6354ea4adc14a: MANILA, Nov 8 — The Philippines’ foreign ministry issued a rare rebuke to government officials and agencies today over public comments about China, stressing the need for a unified voice as the country heads into a key regional summit.

The uniformed services of the Philippines have been engaged in a long-running war of words with the Chinese government over the South China Sea, a busy waterway that Beijing claims almost entirely despite an international ruling that its position has no legal basis.
Multiple senators also called last month for Beijing’s ambassador to be declared persona non grata after he suggested China could “easily win” any confrontation with the Philippines.
Beijing subsequently accused Manila of “erecting multiple obstacles” to its attendance at an Asean defence ministers’ meeting, pointedly sending only an embassy defence attaché.

“Public statements that undermine the government’s diplomatic approach do more than complicate the work of our diplomats,” the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) said, without specifying particular incidents.

“They risk eroding the country’s credibility in international affairs and project an image of internal division that external parties can exploit. Such actions can ultimately weaken the Philippines’ negotiating position.”
The statement specifically addressed the country’s national security establishment and uniformed services, which have engaged in months of heated exchanges with the Chinese Embassy on social media.
US ally the Philippines has been engaged in years of confrontations with China at sea over disputed areas of the strategic waterway, with repeated incidents occurring in recent months.
Today’s statement said that while the armed services were indispensable in documenting incidents, “civilian authority directs the country’s international relations”.

It noted that the 2016 international court verdict that broadly dismissed China’s claims to the South China Sea came via “rigorous legal proceedings under international law, not through public messaging or social media”.
Defence Minister Gilberto Teodoro was banned from visiting China this year, with Beijing citing “irresponsible remarks”.

Chester Cabalza, a Manila-based security analyst, said the foreign ministry had gone public with its message to “assure its counterparts, particularly China, that they are in control of the Philippines’ foreign policy”.
“(The defence department and coast guard) are obliged to carve out the security policy of the country but not its foreign policy. DFA’s statement is an assertion of their role in the bureaucracy.”
China’s top diplomat, Wang Yi, urged the Philippines in a phone call with counterpart Theresa Lazaro last week to rein in politicians who had “smeared” Beijing and crossed its “red lines”.

Lazaro called the conversation “frank and constructive”, adding that “both sides emphasised the need for continued diplomatic dialogue and the proper management of differences anchored on mutual respect”.

Manila is set to host a major Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit next week, with attendees to include US President Donald Trump and recently re-elected Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
Beijing has yet to announce publicly who it will send. — AFP

4653ee39dc8c85d9: SINGAPORE, Nov 8 — Singapore’s 2026 haze episode has cost its economy an estimated S$2.32 billion (RM7.34 billion), exceeding the inflation-adjusted cost of the 2015 crisis despite fewer hazy days and lower average pollution levels, according to a preliminary assessment by two university researchers.
The estimated losses as at October 31 were about 4 per cent higher than the inflation-adjusted S$2.23 billion estimated for 2015, Singapore’s The Business Times reported.

The assessment, by Nanyang Technological University’s Euston Quah and Singapore University of Social Sciences’ Eugene Or, attributed the higher cost to population growth, rising incomes, increased visitor spending and a greater estimated health burden.
Health-related costs, including medical treatment and the economic impact of illness and premature deaths, were higher than in 2015, as were tourism losses.
However, losses from time taken off work and other activities due to illness, along with spending on protective measures such as masks, declined because of the shorter and less severe haze episode.
The assessment also factored in the impact on public well-being, including people’s willingness to pay for cleaner air.
“The sheer scale of this damage strengthens the case for funding prevention alongside tougher penalties,” the researchers said.
Quah and Or suggested that Singapore and other affected countries could help finance alternatives to land clearing by burning, particularly in Indonesia, to reduce the risk of future haze episodes.
Under a proposed “victim-pays” approach, countries affected by haze would contribute towards making fire-free practices more affordable.
“If supporting fire-free practices costs less than the damage avoided, contributing can leave these countries better off,” they said.
The researchers acknowledged that the proposal raised questions of fairness, stressing that companies responsible for fires should still be held accountable.
They also cautioned against treating the estimated economic losses as justification for equivalent spending on prevention.
“A S$2.32 billion haze bill does not automatically justify a S$2.32 billion prevention budget,” they said, calling for phased funding tied to measurable results.
They added that any proposed intervention would also require a thorough cost-benefit analysis to ensure public money was directed towards measures that meaningfully reduced fire risks.
1237d7c03c0ab9df: MELAKA, Nov 8 — Pakatan Harapan (PH) candidate for the Paya Rumput state constituency Datuk Azman Abidin has introduced an initiative to help voters check their polling locations and channels ahead of the 16th Melaka State Election on November 14.

Azman, popularly known as Tok Man, said he and his campaign team would assist voters in checking their polling details while campaigning, with the results printed on small slips and handed to them for reference.

He said the initiative used electoral roll data provided by the Election Commission (EC) to candidates, with the information entered into a system specially developed by PH to facilitate the checking and printing of voter slips.

“Under this initiative, campaign workers only need to enter a voter’s identity card number to retrieve information on their polling location, including the school and assigned polling channel,” he told reporters after attending a courtesy visit and meet-and-greet programme with the Paya Rumput state constituency campaign machinery today.

Also present at the programme, held at the PH Main Operations Room in Krubong here, was PKR Advisory Council chairman Datuk Seri Dr Wan Azizah Wan Ismail, who is also Bandar Tun Razak Member of Parliament.

Azman, who is also the Prime Minister’s Political Secretary, said the idea for the initiative came about after he found that many voters he met during the campaign period could not remember their respective polling centres and channels.

“With this slip, which is more practical than the standard A4-sized printout used previously, voters can not only check their polling details but also keep it in their wallets or pockets for reference again on polling day,” he said.
On the campaign’s progress as it enters its final week, Azman said he would make full use of the remaining time to reach as many residents of the Paya Rumput constituency as possible.

“We will try to cover all areas and reach out to everyone in Paya Rumput, Insha-Allah. The campaign has been going well, in an orderly and peaceful manner. I hope it will remain so until polling day,” he said.
The 16th Melaka State Election will see a three-cornered contest in Paya Rumput between Azman, Rafie Ahmad of Perikatan Nasional (PN) and Abdul Rashid Abu Bakar of Parti Bersama Malaysia (Bersama).
The EC has set Nov 14 as polling day for the Melaka state election, with early voting scheduled for Nov 10.
For the latest news on the 16th Melaka State Election, visit https://election.bernama.com/prn/melaka/2026. — Bernama

One of the fatalities was a British citizen, the PAP news agency reported, citing a police spokesman.
It added that five of the injured were nationals of Germany, Britain, Portugal, Russia and Austria.

d435eeb00b8433c1: BUTTERWORTH, Nov 8 — Penang Sentral, an integrated transport hub and major commercial development, provides a 24-hour waiting area on Level 1 at its stage bus platform, equipped with basic facilities for passengers.
Penang Infrastructure, Transport and Digital Committee chairman Zairil Khir Johari said the facility was intended for passengers waiting for buses or their next connecting transport service.

He said Penang Sentral was operated by Malaysian Resources Corporation Bhd (MRCB) and not the state government, adding that the waiting area was not meant to serve as accommodation or an overnight stay facility.

“MRCB also explained that public access to the terminal is restricted to Level 1 after 1 am, with visitors not allowed to wait or remain in other areas, including the commercial sections and the Urban Transformation Centre (UTC), which are closed for security and operational reasons,” he said when contacted by Bernama today.
He was commenting on a social media post alleging that a passenger had been asked to leave the terminal by security guards after arriving at about 1 am.
The passenger claimed he had been waiting for a ferry to George Town, with his hotel check-in scheduled only for 3 pm the following day.
Feedback from members of the public has also highlighted the need for a dedicated waiting space, particularly for passengers arriving on late-night or early-morning express buses.

University student Hana Nurdira Muhammad Haikal, 20, who studies in Kelantan and frequently returns to Penang during semester breaks, said she often arrived at Penang Sentral early in the morning with her friends, adding that the differing needs of passengers should be taken into consideration.

“I believe MRCB could consider providing a dedicated waiting area for passengers arriving late at night or with early-morning travel schedules. It does not necessarily have to offer accommodation, but should at least have sufficient seating and accessible toilets,” she said.

Kuala Lumpur-based bank officer Shahril Reza Ibrahim, 35, who regularly travels by express bus, said such facilities were important for long-distance passengers, especially those continuing their journeys by ferry.

“MRCB may have its reasons in terms of security and operational control, but from the perspective of user experience, there are still some shortcomings that need to be addressed. As a frequent express bus passenger, I often use Terminal Bersepadu Selatan, which is equipped with a waiting area,” he said.
Penang Sentral serves as an integrated transport hub connecting ferry services, KTM train services, express buses and Rapid Penang buses, with the Mutiara Line LRT also planned to serve the area.

Meanwhile, UTC Seberang Perai, which occupies the third and fourth floors of the terminal and spans more than 60,000 square feet, houses nine government departments, including the Immigration Department and the National Registration Department. — Bernama
b2646eeea28d82ad: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 8 — Godzilla is back, and the King of the Monsters is bringing more than just another round of city-flattening destruction to Malaysian cinemas.

With Godzilla Minus Zero, Oscar-winning director Takashi Yamazaki delivers a sequel that ramps up the visual spectacle, unleashes thunderous sound and, crucially, retains the emotional weight that made its predecessor such a standout.
The follow-up to 2023’s Godzilla Minus One held a premiere screening on November 4 at GSC Mid Valley Megamall, which Malay Mail attended ahead of its nationwide release.

The film sees Godzilla return to wreak havoc, this time with an even greater threat in the form of King Ghidorah, setting the stage for a spectacular clash between two of cinema’s most iconic monsters.
But beneath the destruction lies a more intimate story about survival, family and the lingering scars of war.

The sequel also builds on Japan’s Tokusatsu tradition — a style of filmmaking associated with special effects, miniatures and elaborate creature designs — while embracing the possibilities of modern visual effects technology.

For Yamazaki, whose Godzilla Minus One won the Academy Award for Best Visual Effects in 2024, the challenge is no longer simply making Godzilla look convincing. It is making the spectacle feel bigger without losing the human story.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A battle-scarred Godzilla advances towards Matsumoto City in ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’. — Picture via YouTube/Toho screengrab
Bigger spectacle, deeper emotions
Visually, Godzilla Minus Zero is a considerable step up from its predecessor, with more elaborate destruction sequences, intricate creature designs and an even greater sense of scale.
Godzilla himself has rarely looked more imposing. Every movement carries an enormous sense of weight, while the destruction left in his wake makes his presence feel genuinely terrifying.
King Ghidorah proves an equally formidable presence, with a menacing design that brings a new dimension to the film’s monster-on-monster spectacle.
The result is a series of action sequences that demand to be experienced on the biggest screen possible.
The sound design is just as impressive.
Godzilla’s unmistakable roar and devastating atomic breath attacks reverberate through the cinema, giving the destruction an almost physical intensity.
At the IMAX screening, the sound was reportedly powerful enough to trigger repeated loud-noise notifications on some audience members’ smartwatches.
The orchestral score adds another layer of tension, building a sense of impending catastrophe even before the monsters appear.
Yet for all its technical wizardry, Godzilla Minus Zero understands that destruction alone does not make a compelling film.

Like its predecessor, the sequel places ordinary people at the centre of extraordinary events, allowing the consequences of Godzilla’s rampage to extend beyond collapsing buildings and devastated cities.

Where Godzilla Minus One explored the physical and psychological devastation of war, the new film follows survivors attempting to rebuild their lives, restore their families and confront another catastrophe while still carrying the trauma of the past.

Ryunosuke Kamiki and Minami Hamabe return as Kōichi Shikishima and Noriko Ōishi, alongside familiar faces Hidetaka Yoshioka and Min Tanaka. The cast also features new additions Masami Nagasawa and Jun Kunimura.
Their performances provide an emotional anchor amid the mayhem, giving audiences a reason to care about the people caught in Godzilla’s path.
It is this balance between spectacle and storytelling that makes the sequel particularly effective.

Yamazaki embraces the spirit of Tokusatsu while drawing on contemporary filmmaking technology, demonstrating how Japanese monster cinema can evolve without losing the qualities that made it distinctive.
The result is a film that celebrates its cinematic roots while confidently pushing into new territory.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
The November 4 premiere of ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ at GSC Mid Valley Megamall, Kuala Lumpur. — Picture courtesy of Toho
A monster opening
Godzilla Minus Zero has already made box-office history in Japan.
The film earned ¥910 million (approximately RM26.4 million) on November 3, setting a new opening-day record for a live-action film in the country.
According to Toho, the Japanese studio behind the franchise, it drew more than 590,000 moviegoers on its first day, with attendance more than double that of Godzilla Minus One.
The impressive debut gives the sequel an early boost as it rolls out internationally, although whether it can sustain that momentum and match its predecessor’s critical success remains to be seen.
For Malaysian audiences, the film offers a particularly compelling reason to head to the cinema, especially in IMAX, where its visual scale and thunderous sound can be fully appreciated.
More importantly, Godzilla Minus Zero proves there is still room for genuine human drama amid the monsters and mayhem.
The King of the Monsters may be the main attraction, but it is the people fighting to survive him who give the spectacle its heart.
Godzilla Minus Zero is now showing in Malaysian cinemas, including IMAX.

29935facceb8afa0: HONG KONG, Nov 8 — Philippines trailblazer Alex Eala fell agonisingly short of winning a second WTA Tour title as she lost the Hong Kong Open final to unseeded Claire Liu today.
The American ranked 102 powered past the second seed 6-3, 6-0 for the first title of her career and did not drop a set all week.
Despite being the underdog, the 26-year-old broke in the eighth game of the first set for a 5-3 lead at Victoria Park.
The American squandered the first set point but gobbled up the second to leave the large number of Eala fans in the arena stunned.
Eala, 21, who needed medical treatment and had a large bandage on her right knee, was immediately under pressure on her own serve at the start of the second set.
Liu eventually broke after an attritional opening game to grab the lead and, with that, Eala’s resistance was broken.
Eala, at a career-high 17 in the world, had been seeking to win another title to go with the one she clinched in Washington, DC, in August.
That victory made her the first player from the Philippines to win a tournament on the WTA Tour. — AFP
f55fb26b548abcef: MELAKA, Nov 8 —Kota Laksamana has the potential to become the new state capital of Melaka due to rapid development that can catalyse economic growth and transform the state's landscape, says Melaka Chief Minister Datuk Seri Ab Rauf Yusoh.
He said the state government has formulated a five-year development plan for the area and will work alongside the private sector to realise that potential.

"The plans are in place, but we have yet to integrate them because these concessions were awarded to private companies undertaking projects under the Private Finance Initiative (PFI). This is beyond our control as they have acquired the land.

"However, the state government will coordinate with the private sector, provide necessary support and reduce bureaucracy to accelerate economic activity in Kota Laksamana," he told reporters when met at Jalan Hang Tuah here today.
Ab Rauf said the development plan also encompasses areas under the Straits of Melaka Waterfront Economic Zone (SM-WEZ), covering commercial, residential, healthcare and tourism sectors.
"I appeal to the people to join me in developing Melaka and breathing new life into Kota Laksamana so that it can serve as the new state capital," he said.
Commenting on preparations for the Northeast Monsoon, Ab Rauf said the state government has stepped up disaster preparedness, including identifying 102 flood hotspots across the state.
He said the locations were identified based on records of floods recurring at least three times within three years.
"Preparedness measures include round-the-clock flood monitoring across six major river basins, alongside continuous recording of rainfall data and river water levels.
"The early warning system has also been enhanced with the installation of 14 flood warning sirens and 10 surveillance cameras at strategic locations across Melaka," he added.

Ab Rauf said flood mitigation assets have also been readied, comprising 21 water control gates, 21 pump houses and 14 portable emergency pumps that can be mobilised to critical areas, in addition to monitoring 105 flood retention ponds.
He added that 447 small-scale works worth RM43.8 million have been carried out this year to bolster flood management infrastructure and mitigate disaster risks.
He also advised residents, particularly in coastal areas, to remain vigilant as the high-tide phenomenon expected until Nov 17 could cause flash floods in low-lying areas.
"The state government will continue to issue early alerts and advisories through the Melaka State Disaster Management Committee (JPBN) to ensure effective emergency response," he said. — Bernama

c8a8002b30542aaf: The International Telecommunications Union (ITU) kicks off its quadrennial plenipotentiary on Monday, and internet governance organizations are bracing in case the event becomes a forum for nation-states to try to challenge their roles.

The ITU is the United Nations' specialized agency for information and communication technologies, meaning its members are nation-states. The body's role is to facilitate international connectivity, which it does by managing radio spectrum, satellite orbits, and working on relevant technical standards.

Its key standards are pervasive. ITU-T X.509 sets out the rules of public key infrastructure. ITU-T E.164 governs telephone numbers. ITU-T H.264 and 265 define the video codecs used for most online streams.
The ITU's role is largely uncontested, yet its work gets very close to that of the organizations who work on technologies that make the internet work.

Those bodies include the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF); the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN), which oversees the domain name system; and the regional internet registries (RIRs), which manage IP addresses. The World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) works on HTML, CSS, and accessibility.

Governments participate in work at those internet governance bodies but are just one voice among many and can't override the consensus-driven decision-making process they use, under a system which has come to be known as the multi-stakeholder governance model.

At a 2025 event called WSIS+20, the United Nations endorsed multi-stakeholder governance by deciding that its Internet Governance Forum (IGF) should become a permanent body. That decision effectively endorsed multi-stakeholder governance, and kept the ITU out of internet standards.
Yet the IGF hasn't met since WSIS+20, so it is yet to start operating meaningfully as a permanent body.

This year's ITU meeting is therefore a moment at which stakeholders can stress-test the delicate balance between the ITU, internet governance bodies, and the emerging IGF. Such a test could see ITU members try to have it pursue new fields that overlap with work performed by internet governance organizations.
This has already happened before. China tried to have the ITU work on "New IP" – a major revision to internet protocol, a technology the IETF manages.

In 2022, Russia and China backed a candidate for the ITU presidency who favored giving nations a stronger role in internet governance, potentialy by having the ITU take over some standards work. That candidate was not elected.

Ahead of next week's meetings, the Internet Society published a background paper that declared it is "actively challenging proposals that could affect the Internet's underlying technical architecture or increase fragmentation, as well as those that could affect connectivity, particularly for remote, underserved, and unserved communities."

The society is watching for resolutions on AI, quantum technologies, and other emerging areas that could embed specific technologies in ITU mandates. It also observes that decisions are yet to be made on which bodies should oversee governance of low-earth orbit satellite constellations, submarine cable resilience, and spectrum policy.
ICANN is also watching with interest.
"ICANN welcomes the recognition of the consensus-based WSIS+20 outcomes," the organization told The Register by email.

"At the same time, proposals that seek to expand the ITU's role in areas such as IP-based networks, the Domain Name System, management of Internet resources, and Internet-related public policy issues raise concerns about overlapping mandates and the creation of parallel processes that could affect the health of the Internet."
ICANN didn't point to any specific proposals that raise such concerns, and at ITU meetings most proposals – of which there are 278 this time around – are decided on consensus.
It is, however, possible for ITU members to amend proposals during meetings, leaving open the possibility of significant policy changes coming up for a vote during the 18 days the event occupies. ®

6ea945f382f18776: From Ibrahim M Ahmad
The dispute over former prime minister Najib Razak’s proposed transfer from Kajang Prison to house arrest is no longer simply about whether he should go home.

At its core, the controversy raises a broader question: what happens when a royal pardon, a court order and a separate criminal sentence intersect in ways that existing laws do not clearly anticipate?

The latest developments have placed the Attorney-General’s Chambers (AGC), the prisons department, Najib’s lawyers and even Istana Negara on seemingly different sides of a debate over implementation rather than principle. All parties say they are attempting to uphold the law. The disagreement is over what the law, and the Yang di-Pertuan Agong's decree, require in practice.
That distinction is important.

Public discussion has largely centred on whether Najib should be released from prison immediately. Yet the more significant issue may be whether Malaysia’s legal framework adequately addresses a situation in which a prisoner is granted a conditional royal pardon while also facing another custodial sentence.

The King’s position appears straightforward. Najib was granted a conditional pardon allowing him to serve the remainder of his SRC International sentence under house arrest, provided he paid the RM50 million fine imposed by the court. That condition has now been met.
Ordinarily, that would appear to settle the matter.

However, the High Court document issued following payment of the fine has introduced uncertainty over the legal effect of Najib’s "discharge" and whether the SRC sentence continues to run until 2028 or is regarded as completed.

The document, called an “Order of Discharge on Payment of Fine”, directs that Najib be discharged immediately. But it also states that the remainder of his sentence is to be served under house arrest until Aug 23, 2028.

The question is what “discharged” means in this context. Does it mean he should leave Kajang Prison and continue serving his SRC sentence at home? Or could it mean that the SRC sentence is legally complete? The AGC says clarification is needed on the effect of the order.
The distinction is far from academic.

Najib’s separate 15-year prison sentence in the 1MDB case was ordered to begin only after the SRC sentence ends. If the SRC sentence continues under house arrest, the chronology is uncomplicated. If it is deemed complete upon payment of the fine, questions arise about whether the 1MDB sentence should begin immediately.
Faced with that uncertainty, the AGC argues that clarification is needed before any transfer takes place.

Critics may see this as an unnecessary delay, particularly after Istana Negara stated that all conditions of the pardon had been fulfilled. Supporters of the AGC’s position, however, contend that resolving ambiguity now is preferable to triggering fresh legal challenges later.
Neither argument is entirely without merit.

What the episode has exposed is a potential gap in Malaysia’s legal architecture. While imprisonment, parole and remission are governed by established laws and procedures, house arrest remains relatively unfamiliar territory. There is no comprehensive statutory framework setting out how such arrangements should operate, how compliance should be monitored or how they interact with other criminal sentences.
That absence has created room for competing interpretations.

The issue also extends beyond Najib himself. Any legal principles established in his case could influence how future pardons are implemented and how exceptional forms of custody are administered. For that reason, the courts’ eventual interpretation may carry implications beyond one high-profile prisoner.
At the same time, there is a public confidence dimension that cannot be ignored.

Najib’s status as a former prime minister means every development is scrutinised through the lens of equality before the law. Many Malaysians will want assurance that whatever outcome emerges is grounded in clear legal principles rather than political considerations or institutional pressure.
That makes transparency critical.
The public deserves a clear explanation of how the pardon is meant to operate, how the prison and court orders interact, and how the separate 1MDB sentence fits into the equation.

Ultimately, the dispute should not become a contest between institutions. The King’s decree, the courts and the executive branch each have defined constitutional roles. The challenge lies in ensuring those roles operate coherently when they overlap.

The immediate question is whether Najib leaves prison or remains there for the time being. The more enduring question is whether Malaysia’s legal system can provide a clear and consistent answer when faced with circumstances that its laws did not expressly anticipate.
That is an issue that extends well beyond Najib Razak.
Ibrahim M Ahmad is an FMT reader.
